#4279. 10 Metroidvanias With the Most Nominations at The Game Awards

Ronald is a video game journalist with more than 10 years of experience in the industry, working on several of the most important Spanish websites.

Although Metroidvanias have been largely dominated by indie games since video game award ceremonies became commonplace, this hasn't diminished their presence at the industry's most important gala events.

Today, the indie ecosystem is just as capable as AAA titles of delivering masterpieces, which has led to them gaining a more prominent role whenever we gather to review each year's best releases.

Certainly, it's not as prominent a genre as RPGs or pure action-adventure games, but it has still had enough presence to demonstrate that it's a variant that has nothing to envy in the legitimacy of others.

Therefore, clarifying beforehand that several titles will be omitted for sharing the last spot with only one nomination, prioritizing instead those that were most relevant, these are the ten Metroidvanias with the most nominations at The Game Awards.

Along with another title that will be featured later, Axiom Verge marks the first year a Metroidvania earned a nomination; in this case, for Best Independent Game of 2015.

Although it had to contend with notable releases like the global phenomenon Rocket League and the indie gem Undertale, Tom Happ secured his place in the genre's history thanks to his magnificent science fiction journey.

In an era when Metroidvanias hadn't yet established themselves as a major force, this solo developer created such a captivating title that, to this day, it still has few direct competitors in its craftsmanship, as it is truly unique.

Nothing would please me more today than an Axiom Verge 3, so this is a fitting opportunity to recall the historic feat achieved by the first entry and ask Happ to consider repeating that glory soon.

As a living legend of contemporary Metroidvanias, single-handedly setting the course for the genre in the decade following its release, Hollow Knight couldn't be left off this list.

However, contrary to what one might think today, Team Cherry's creation only received a nomination for Best Indie Debut in 2017, which it lost to a colossus that, upon its release, made a greater impact: Cuphead.

Even so, time would gradually vindicate this masterpiece, whose aura would extend to all subsequent developments, rewriting history in the memories of many who recall, albeit mistakenly, that it was nominated in more categories.

The power of hindsight is undeniable when the subject is a title with Hollow Knight's legacy, which also highlights how indie games, over the years, have become increasingly respected and taken seriously in these spaces.

From indies to multiplayers, these ten video games that defined the 2010s shaped the industry as we know it today.

Leaving aside the inevitable debate about Dead Cells as a Metroidvania, Motion Twin made history by being one of the first games in the genre to receive multiple nominations at The Game Awards.

Historically, this fusion of the genre with the roguelike philosophy earned the second Metroidvania award in the event's history by winning Best Action Game in 2018, though it lost the Best Independent Game category to the acclaimed Celeste.

In the category it won, it faced stiff competition from titanic blockbusters like Call of Duty: Black Ops 4, Destiny 2: Forsaken, and Far Cry 5, though this didn't prevent what would eventually become one of the best-selling indie games of all time from taking home the prize.

The recognition is, of course, more than deserved, given that few titles in the last decade are capable of generating the excitement and addictiveness that Dead Cells produces, so no matter how many AAA games they had put against it, it would have won anyway.

That high-caliber developers like Ubisoft are investing in the genre to revitalize their longest-running franchises is a relatively new trend, yet it yielded definitive results with Prince of Persia: The Lost Crown.

The presence of a game in the genre with such a strong production value allowed it to win an unprecedented honor for Metroidvanias, the Innovation in Accessibility Award in 2024, although it lost the Best Action-Adventure Game category to Astro Bot.

Regardless, it was the first medal at The Game Awards that the French developer received after winning Best Sim/Strategy Game with Mario + Rabbids: Sparks of Hope in 2022, making its impact in terms of recognition significant.

Furthermore, it's an extraordinary video game with a superb level of polish and freshness, so hopefully Ubisoft will recognize this trend and begin to replicate what they did with Prince of Persia: The Lost Crown with several of their most forgotten and missed IPs.

2024 was a fertile year for indie games, and although it didn't win either of the categories it was nominated for—because Balatro is larger than life—Animal Well remains in the collective imagination as an unparalleled masterpiece.

As part of the nominees for Best Independent Game and Best Indie Debut in 2024, Billy Basso stood tall with his iconic solo project against giants of the indie ecosystem like Devolver Digital, Kepler Interactive, and Annapurna Interactive without hesitation.

Basso picks up the mantle from Happ and doubles Axiom Verge's achievement almost a decade later, doing so with a game that defies Metroidvania conventions and replaces all combat with countless intricate yet wonderful puzzles that completely immerse you in the adventure.

Two years later, Animal Well remains one of my most cherished memories of the entire decade, and I think it will likely stay there for... a lifetime.

From the hops and dashes in Hollow Knight to the integral platforming of Pseudoregalia, these are 10 Metroidvanias with satisfying platforming.

The first of this list's five Metroidvanias to be nominated for three or more awards is none other than Tunic, the indie gem that swept through audiences and critics alike in 2022, establishing itself among the genre's most outstanding representatives this generation.

Unfortunately, its nominations for Best Independent Game, Best Action-Adventure Game, and Best Indie Debut in 2022 didn't result in any badges, as it was up against GOTY contenders like Stray and God of War: Ragnarök, though this only underscores its impressive quality.

That essence reminiscent of The Legend of Zelda didn't go unnoticed, and it underpinned the structure of one of recent years' most exciting and intriguing adventures, particularly because of its decision not to hold your hand and instead rely on your ability to find your way through combat, exploration, and puzzle-solving.

The fact that Tunic is the first video game from its developers is absolutely incredible, and that under said conditions it achieved three nominations on the most anticipated night in the video game industry is quite high recognition.

As one of the most exquisite audiovisual expressions the genre has witnessed since its inception, Ori and the Will of the Wisps was an inevitable presence on any list of this caliber.

Moon Studios' sequel was among the nominees for Best Art Direction, Best Music, and Best Action-Adventure Game in 2020, though unfortunately, it had to compete against absolute generational masterpieces like Ghost of Tsushima, Final Fantasy VII Remake, and The Last of Us Part II.

However, as with Tunic, Ori and the Will of the Wisps being considered alongside numerous video games that have defined the decade is one of the greatest displays of Metroidvania greatness on the big stage.

It's no wonder the title consistently appears on lists of the best of its kind, and one that would have completely swept its categories had it been nominated in years less dominated by modern classics.

Metroid Dread made history as the first Metroidvania to be nominated for Game of the Year in 2021, and for many it was the true winner of the category that, ultimately, went to It Takes Two.

Regardless of the debate, MercurySteam solidified its relationship with Nintendo by bringing Samus Aran back to 2D, reinforcing it as the natural home of the iconic bounty hunter by delivering a near-perfect creation.

It was also nominated for Best Action-Adventure Game, which it won, and for Players’ Voice, which it lost, thus becoming the second game in the genre to win a category after Dead Cells, despite probably deserving more.

The mother of all the entries on this list is an inseparable part of its history, and although perhaps not to the fullest extent, its participation in The Game Awards is a recognition of that legacy.

From the ever-challenging Celeste to some surprisingly difficult gems, these are the 10 Hardest Indie Games To 100% Complete.

With four nominations and one victory, Ori and the Blind Forest is pure Metroidvania history, bursting onto the scene at the interactive industry's most prestigious awards ceremony as the genre's first appearance (alongside Axiom Verge).

Developed by a much smaller team than when they collaborated with Microsoft on the sequel, and as a less experienced studio within a still largely unexplored genre, the project was nominated for Best Independent Game, Best Art Direction, Best Score, and Best Action-Adventure in 2015.

Of all the nominations, it took home the award for its visual direction, beating out Bloodborne, The Witcher 3: Wild Hunt, and Metal Gear Solid 5: The Phantom Pain, one of the biggest surprises the ceremony has ever seen.

While this is a more common and normal occurrence these days, the fact that Ori and the Blind Forest achieved such a strong presence, and even managed to win an award among a couple of candidates for best game of all time, is simply beyond belief.

What I consider the best Metroidvania of all time is also the most recognized game in the genre at The Game Awards, leaving Hollow Knight: Silksong with the most nominations at six, though it only managed one win.

Game of the Year, Best Art Direction, Best Score and Music, Best Independent Game, Players’ Voice, and Best Action-Adventure Game were the categories in which Team Cherry's unimaginable sequel was nominated, ultimately taking home the last one.

Like Ori and the Blind Forest, Hornet had to overcome giants such as Death Stranding 2: On the Beach, Ghost of Yotei, and Split Fiction to win the award, a remarkable achievement considering the team is still just three people.

In the categories it didn't win, it was surpassed by the now-legendary Clair Obscur: Expedition 33, which took home four of the six awards in which it shared nominations, and Wuthering Waves, which won the user vote.

In any case, Hollow Knight: Silksong is the Metroidvania with the most nominations at The Game Awards, and it's tough to imagine when we'll see another title that can match such a record.

From classics like Teslagrad to modern gems like Blasphemous, these are ten Metroidvania franchises that should come back in 2027.

#4278. Battlefield 6's next season will speed up battle pass progression, and make it so Redsec players who don't own the game can actually make progress

Season 2 of Battlefield 6 looks to bring a host of broad, positive changes to XP, progression, audio and more.

Ahead of the start of Battlefield 6’s Season 2 next week, Battlefield Studios has shared some insight into a few of the major goals the developer has with the Season 2 patch. The game’s second season was delayed in mid-January, and the developer even brought back Battlefield Labs to test out some of the new content and features coming with the new season.

Indeed, the broader goals BF Studios shared with players in a new blog post reflect some of what Labs players already went hands-on with, while others are the result of work on long-standing issues with both the game itself, as well as free-to-play mode Redsec.

We know that Season 2 is introducing a big new map to the game, Contaminated, which the developer has been teasing. The map will indeed arrive in the first part of the season, and it’s going to do so alongside a new LTM that “introduces a new element of tactics.” A second, “high-intensity map” will debut later into the season, alongside another LTM where players battle through an underground base, in darkness.

The real meat of the blog post, however, covers the broader gameplay changes everyone will see once the new season kicks off. There’s a massive focus on player progression, especially when it concerns free-to-play Redsec players.

Challenges are being streamlined yet again, with more broad parameters that don’t require specific modes. Some, like dailies, will also allow for assists to count towards their criteria. Less restrictive challenges are welcome, but even more so is the faster battle pass progression.

BF Studios is changing the rate at which battle pass Tokens are earned from career XP, and making it so they’re earnable by playing the game normally, and by completing weekly challenges. These changes should also help Redsec players, who will also benefit from faster career and weapon XP earn rates - across both battle royale, and Gauntlet. In general, the career experience should feel more rewarding, especially for earlier ranks.

Weapon balance and recoil are two areas that will continue to evolve in Battlefield 6, it seems, and Season 2 is specifically tackling recoil patterns to make them more consistent when you compensate for them.

Movement is being adjusted with the Season 2 patch, too, though thankfully it’s limited to general feel that touches areas like vaulting, ladder transitions, and acceleration curves. You should also see better continuity and consistency between animations and feel.

Audio is getting a pass with the upcoming patch, especially when it comes to footstep and interaction audio. This also extends to something the developer has been working on improving for a while, and it has to do with how the game decides which audio tracks to prioritise in busy situations.

Tomorrow, the full Battlefield 6 Season 2 trailer will be released, while a more detailed roadmap is expected by the end of this week.

#4277. Interview: Petit Planet dev team talks life vs management, and the ultimate introvert's dream

Time to stop and smell the roses, so to speak

So-called "cosy" life sims are a dime a dozen these days, but HoYoverse is looking to throw its hat in the ring with a different kind of approach to your average entry in the genre. For one thing, it's supposedly a true life sim, not a management sim. And for another, it's really all about slowing down and unwinding at the end of the day, not looking for an alternate life apart from your own.

Honestly, that kind of low-pressure vibe feels like exactly what I need at the moment to help me deal with the hustle and bustle of everyday life, and over the past week, we've had the pleasure of spending a few days with the Petit Planet team to share with us what that's all about.

It was a privilege to hear lead game designer Murphy and lead artist Yinli Huang's thoughts at the roundtable discussion we had during the media tour in Seoul, South Korea, including their own hopes and dreams for the life sim (I've edited their answers for clarity and brevity, by the way). It's interesting to see such a different take on the genre, for instance, especially since the entire "world" is structured into mini-planets rather than your typical town or city. It was initially made as a flat space, but it wasn't in line with the team's core design.

"As a life simulation game, we decided to use some rendering techniques to present a feeling of that sphere. That indeed brought a lot of challenges technically and visually." One of those challenges was actually how to make it so that players don't feel any kind of motion sickness across this spherical world.

And it's certainly a very different style when compared to other HoYoverse games. "It's very important for HoYoverse to explore different genres, and with a life simulation game, it's the kind of genre where we can build an emotional connection with players and the community. And from HoYoverse's past experiences, we've accumulated a lot of knowledge in terms of technology and the ability to build out narratives and characters. We believe that those capabilities developed from our past games can bring brand-new experiences for players of this genre."

This is evident in the difference from, say, Animal Crossing, as the team believes Petit Planet is, as I mentioned, a life sim and not a management sim. It's meant to be cosier and less pressure-filled, which, as someone who doesn't have the patience to grind through a management sim, I greatly appreciate. But what makes Petit Planet still inherently HoYoverse is, as the team puts it, that quality that players have come to know and expect from the brand.

"We always try to provide high-quality games to our players, and that is also what Petit Planet wants to do. And in Petit Planet, we've also tried to explore something new - the multiplayer gaming experience and also a social system - and that is something unique to this game."

Still, from what I've played, it did feel like the single-player aspect is robust enough as it is, which is interesting for a life sim like this. "For us, it's very important to provide a good gaming experience for both types of players. For those who prefer to play solo, there are always settings that will allow them to turn off those multiplayer experiences, but once they feel comfortable or they want to explore the social part of the game, they can always go to the Galactic Bazaar and also use the Epistolarian's Desk. But the core gameplay will be largely the same for both types of players," they explained.

"We have adopted certain technical measures to make sure the multiplayer experience will go as smoothly as possible. For example, when a player gets to the Galactic Bazaar, the multiplayer settings will adjust dynamically based on the number of players. But there will also be some limits when players visit other planets - you can choose to allow or ban players from taking resources from your planet."

Which actually brings me to the most interesting bit for me with my hands-on experience, which is the aforementioned Epistolarian's Desk. I asked them what the inspiration or story behind that was, because I felt like that was what resonated with me the most as an introvert. I really like the idea of writing a letter and the uncertainty of whether or not you'll receive a reply, and seeing all the letters that all of the people have written so far.

There's just something so heartbreaking and tragic - yet still so inherently beautiful about it.

I told the team that the system felt very considerate, as you're always asking for permission if people are allowed to reply or if you're going to accept their reply. I just wanted to know the inspiration behind the idea, because I don't think I've seen that anywhere else before.

"It's a kind of asynchronous design on purpose, because that kind of system won't bring our players, especially introverts, too much pressure. We've also looked at similar references in other places, but we found that players will message randomly, so we tried to set up a formal setting in the game to make the action more like a ritual. This means that people can then write a letter and take it more seriously," the team shared. "We designed the exchange on purpose because we found that the constant need to interact might put pressure on players. Once you become friends online in a game, you will need to invest a lot of energy and time to sustain the friendship, so we want to avoid that in Petit Planet."

This actually extends further to dailies and seasonal content - with Petit Planet being a live service sim, how can the team make sure the dailies aren't a grind and still keep seasonal content fresh? Mobai, the NPC sheepdog, even jokes that there's no mortgage here, after all.

"We'd like to use the fishing system as an example. So, in some other games, you might develop skills and levels for your fishing skills. But for Petit Planet, whether you're a new player or a veteran player, the fish that you get is the same - it's random. So there's no growth curve; we want to make it simulate real life, so the fish you get will vary depending on the season or the weather. Our purpose is to provide a little surprise for players every time they log in to the game, so that they will have the incentive to log in and enjoy the experience."

The narrative goes hand in hand here as well. "Unlike other HoYoverse games, there's no such thing as a 'main plot'. The whole narrative will be more fragmented - for example, if you look at the descriptions for the items, there will be a lot of content or stories behind them. We've also developed a very comprehensive backstory of each of the Neighbors - that is also part of the main narrative, because we want to make this a more livable world."

Now, all that cosiness is all well and good, but one of the things I was also curious about, especially with my experience of the beta, was how the controls worked in this supposedly more intentional, mindful world. I know that developers said they designed some of the controls to be "less automatic" - for lack of a better term - to force players to pay closer attention to what they're doing, which is something I also observed while playing.

For instance, I noticed that you really can't simply jump across ledges, as you really need to go around to find the door or the right pathway should you need to. So I asked them how they're able to balance those "less automatic" controls with making sure things aren't frustrating for players when the controls start to get wonkier than usual.

"In terms of controls and cameras, we did a lot of research and considered different solutions, from the most limited ones to allowing players to freely explore the landscape and environment. We thought of different degrees of freedom for players while also keeping the imperfections for the life simulation. The team debated different solutions for, say, climbing. Initially, internally, we discussed how many layers a player can climb, but there will be different creatures on the lower level and higher level, so if players can jump multiple layers at once, that will remove the joy of exploring and the sense of surprise. So there are deliberate considerations behind the control of players in Petit Planet."

With that, we wrapped things up - and I do have to say that so far, Petit Planet is shaping up to be a dream come true. I've never really connected with life sims and management sims before, as I've always found the fetch quests and social aspects a tad too grindy for me. Thankfully, Petit Planet seems to be offering a gentler way for us all to enjoy a virtual world without the demands that usually come with it, and with its launch on December 4th, we'll get to see if that is indeed the case.

For now, if you're curious about how it plays, I did a quick preview of Petit Planet when it was in its beta phase earlier this year, and I'll have a proper review ready in time for its release soon too. And since its monetisation is supposedly purely for cosmetics only, I'd say it's worth giving a go - especially if you're the ultimate introvert like me.

We still don't know exactly when The Elder Scrolls VI: Sentinel will be released, but we're now about seven years from its original announcement at E3 2018.

#4274. Petit Planet - 5 reasons why it's definitely not another Animal Crossing

Petit Planet offers a gentler, kinder, and more considerate world - and right now, maybe that's exactly what we need

I felt seen. That's generally the vibe I got from Petit Planet during my time with it, but honestly, it might not seem so obvious at first glance. For one thing, the cosy life sim is extremely similar to Nintendo's Animal Crossing, and for another, simulating a virtual life outside the daily grind is nothing new.

But at the HoYoverse Media Tour 2026 in Seoul, I got the chance to get to know Petit Planet with all its complexities and so-called deliberate "imperfections" on a more personal level, and these apparent flaws are, in essence, what makes it more beautiful - much like in real life.

Now, I already did my time as a Planet Tender six months ago during Petit Planet's initial beta, but after going hands-on with the life sim again and experiencing the advanced content during the event, I've come away with a handful of reasons why I now see it's not just another entry into an already saturated genre. It's a tad unfortunate that it took a second go for it to dawn on me, but don't they say that love is sweeter the second time around?

You're responsible for your rose planet The first and likely most obvious difference between this and the aforementioned Nintendo property is the fact that the entire world is, well, a world - albeit on a (seemingly) much smaller scale. You're a Planet Tender, responsible for tending to your very own mini-planet across a charming, spherical space. When I spoke to the Petit Planet devs, they mentioned that this is one of their core design principles, which is why despite the technical challenges that come with rendering something like this (not to mention the possibility of players getting motion sickness), the team pushed themselves to make it work to the best of their ability.

And it really does work. Navigating your mini-planet feels lovingly personal, like you're really tending to something that's truly your own, making every crop you harvest, fish you catch, and decor you place much more intentional. I definitely see what HoYoverse is trying to do there - by shrinking the scale down to a smaller and more manageable size, they're able to evoke all sorts of feels. It's essentially an exercise in learning to be more mindful, which is exactly Petit Planet's theme. Life sim, not management sim The team was quick to reiterate that there's a big difference between a life sim and a management sim, because Petit Planet is definitely not the latter. Your self-contained world aside, dailies don't give you any FOMO; they're less pressure-filled, and you're not meant to speedrun through your tasks like they're chores. Mobai, the official "tutorial" Neighbor who's a totally chill sheepdog, even tells you there's no mortgage to pay back here, poking fun at demanding NPCs other management sims have.

I feel like this ties perfectly well with the more emotional aspect of your smaller home - giving it all kinds of TLC never feels like a burden, because you're never pressured to compete or perform, never hounded to optimise numbers, never pushed or overwhelmed by the to-do list that's practically breathing down your neck. It's a gentler, kinder, and more considerate experience, which brings me to my next point. Consent is everything One major thing I noticed was that the system is almost always asking for your permission, which, as an introvert, I appreciate so darn much. I'm someone who struggles with a bit of phone anxiety, as every time the phone rings - no matter who's calling - I get a mini-panic attack for a split second. I've never really fully understood why that's so, but I suppose it has something to do with how intrusive and sudden a phone call can be to an introvert's alone time.

In essence, Petit Planet - while offering robust experiences for both solo players and social butterflies alike - doesn't really shove the multiplayer aspect down your throat. Social systems are opt-in and not mandatory, so you can choose to go at it alone if you ever feel the need to recharge your social battery all by yourself. You can allow or deny other players from visiting or taking resources from your planet, and you can even choose the stage of your relationships whenever you see someone else's planet floating by overhead.

I found this incredibly refreshing, especially with the Epistolarian's Desk. It's a letter-writing system where you can write notes and send them out there into the Starsea, and whether or not you receive a reply is never certain. I love how melancholy this whole act is - the idea of sending a letter to someone and never quite knowing if you'll ever get a response back. It's bittersweet and beautiful, and one of the ways I feel Petit Planet invites you to slow down and be more mindful in life.

So yes, the loneliness is real, but there's comfort in knowing someone's out there going through the same thing too. Live service without the grind But probably the most striking thing that makes Petit Planet stand out is the fact that it's a live service game, which is an interesting mix. Yes, it's all about slowing down, but it's also got constant updates to keep things fresh - and I guess I'll just have to wait until the official launch to see how that goes. Updates are supposedly going to be released at a more relaxed pace, with a focus on daily pleasures and fresh surprises you'll get to experience every time you log in.

For example, I was able to play through the winter content for the advanced build I played at the event, and there was a whole bunch of stuff to do for the seasonal update. But again, I didn't feel pressured to cross everything off my checklist of side-quests and missions - I found that I could simply wander around and kick snowballs at random things if I wanted to, just because. The new Neighbors are a lovely touch, of course, and if you ever feel like you want to get to know them a little bit better, you definitely can - or not; it's all up to you. Neighbors aren't pets Given that this is a HoYoverse game, I know some people might think that the Neighbors are part of a gacha system where you have to pull to collect them all, but the NPCs here aren't pets you need to unlock to progress. Neighbors have their own different personalities, quirks, and homes, with interactions you can trigger (even among each other) depending on certain events. They remember answers too and have their own preferences for their home decor, so they're definitely not a thing you own!

And if they're not part of the gacha, this means that monetisation is purely for cosmetics only, which is in line with the low-key nature of the sim. Even the Starsea Voyage - a mode where you can go around and explore uncharted lands for lovely little discoveries - no longer uses up resources, as you can simply wander the Starsea and do some introverting if you want to. It's all about relaxing and not managing resources, after all, which is also evident in how you navigate the terrain around you.

Interestingly, the devs included deliberate "imperfections" in the way you control your character. Controls are a tad clumsy in some places, as they wanted to avoid entirely automated affairs to force you to pay more attention. I did notice this while I was playing, as I found I couldn't just randomly scale higher ledges or climb through them just to get to where I needed to go - I had to really go around and look for the stairs or the right pathways, making things more intentional.

I'm curious to see how this will resonate with players, as clumsy controls run the risk of frustrating everyone. But if it pays off, then it's a massively effective way of keeping players chill on a more subconscious level - and HoYoverse has always been big on taking risks.

Suffice it to say I'm looking forward to the official launch on December 4th, which says a lot since I've never really been a fan of the genre. Whether or not Petit Planet changes all that remains to be seen, but I'm definitely willing to voyage into the Starsea to find out.

#4273. Diablo 4’s next class is the Warlock, but you can sort of play it today in Diablo 2: Resurrected’s new DLC

Blizzard has officially unveiled the Warlock, the second class coming to Diablo 4 with Lord of Hatred.

Diablo 4’s segment in the big Diablo 30th Anniversary Spotlight was among the biggest, even if the reason most of us tuned in was somewhat spoiled earlier in the same livestream. Blizzard unveiled the Warlock, the second of two classes coming to the game with the upcoming Lord of Hatred expansion.

The first class, being the Paladin, is already available to play for anyone who pre-ordered the expansion, but the Warlock won’t be accessible until the expansion arrives in late April.

The Warlocks are positioned as the opposite of the Paladins, in that they don’t mind utilising forbidden knowledge, drawing on the powers of Hell itself to fight its own overlords. The Warlock is the edgy, antihero counterpart to the Paladin’s purity and devotion to the Light.

The livestream did not show off any Warlock gameplay, but Blizzard is planning a dedicated livestream to show off the new class’ gameplay, and dig deeper into its lore and abilities. That show is scheduled for March 5.

What we did get to see was our first look at Skovos, the expansion’s new region. This Mediterranean-inspired location is where the new story arc will unfold, but it’s also being positioned as the endgame destination for Diablo 4 once the credits roll.

Lord of Hatred, of course, as previously revealed, introduces two new endgame modes in War Plans, and Echoing Hatred.

War Plans lets you create a custom playlist of up to five endgame activities to target specific rewards and create your own experience. There’s a new activity tree that works with all endgame activities, and creating War Plans is how you earn progression there.

Echoing Hatred, on the other hand, is a rare event that pits you against legions of Mephisto’s minions. It’s triggered through a rare lootable item that unlocks access. It’s essentially horde mode; where you’ll face unending waves of enemies, though not without a couple of twists.

We also got a bit more colour on the expanded class skill trees, which all players will benefit from when the expansion arrives. The Talisman system, which unlocks set bonuses, was also shown off. And, of course, the return of the iconic Horadric Cube, which gives you control over Affixes.

The Anniversary Spotlight should’ve had a Year of the Warlock subtitle, because the class is also making its way to both Diablo Immortal, as well as Diablo 2: Resurrected. The showcase revealed the Reign of the Warlock DLC, which adds the aforementioned Warlock to D2R - its first new class in 25 years.

Reign of the Warlock, which is available now in D2R, also makes a few updates to the game, such as new quality of life features, the Colossal Ancients endgame encounter, updated Terror Zones and more. You also get some cosmetics in Diablo 4 if you purchase this expansion.

#4269. Afterwords – Marvel’s Wolverine

We interviewed game director Mike Daly after the launch of Insomniac’s recent Wolverine game to get his take on what makes Wolverine and Spidey different to work on, his thoughts on breadcrumb trails, and why Logan can’t ever seem to get the girl.

Insomniac had extensive experience working on well-known superhero characters before starting on Wolverine. Early on, what traits or qualities of Logan as a story character and playable avatar did you know you wanted to focus on, distinct from the Spider-Man games and character?

From a story perspective, we wanted Logan to be a man with centuries of experiences that he can’t remember, creating a mix of being worn, wizened, and cynical. His resilience makes him fearless, which comes through in his candid manner, and he can’t ignore his sense of justice, as much as he would like to.

For gameplay, it was important that players felt the difference made by his healing factor, claws, berserker rage, animalistic strength, enhanced senses, his adamantium skeleton, and corresponding weight.

In both story and gameplay, emotionally and physically, Wolverine is a hero who gets hurt and feels that pain deeply but always gets back up again and presses on. This dogged resilience was really important to us and a central theme of story and gameplay.

Wolverine is more of a linear adventure than the open-world exploration of a big city seen in Spidey. In my playthrough, that added to the sense of relentless pacing that characterizes Wolverine as a fictional lead. Was that part of the thinking behind why the game was built that way, or was the more linear path there for other reasons?

Ultimately, we made a game suited for a Wolverine story that had comic book pacing – action and meaningful story development on every page.

We experimented with different structures and stories, evaluating from the perspective of: “Is this the best way to do Wolverine justice?” As the various things we tried didn’t feel right, we had to challenge our assumptions and look to our favorite Wolverine stories for inspiration, which led us to where we ended up – a story with momentum in which every beat felt authentic to the character.

Scenes and gameplay sequences that might have been fine in other games but didn’t strongly evoke Wolverine undermined the consistency of the fantasy we were trying to create, so we tried to keep things very focused.

After the game’s release, there was an active online conversation about some of the breadcrumb-trail guidance the game offers to lead you to pickups, or to mark the continued golden path of progression. What was the thinking internally about that design decision, and your take on the debate after the game launched?

Our thinking was that it was essential to make the player feel like they were empowered by Logan’s enhanced senses, a canonical mutant ability, enabling players to do things they could not with other characters. We wanted to weave that power into as many parts of the game as we could, so that if Logan could smell or hear something relevant, the player could see it too.

For collectibles, we wanted players to enjoy seeking out and spotting senses cues, enabling you to find things that would have been obscure to other characters. Using the cues, players can cover a lot of ground without feeling the need to scour, maintaining story and action momentum.

After the game launched, we saw feedback from players that interpreted senses as abstract designer guidance, along with a desire for options in how they approached exploration and discovery. Fortunately, we have been able to incorporate this feedback from players in our post-launch patches. One aspect we’ve improved is the scent trail’s organic presentation, so they give a stronger impression that they belong in the world rather than being an abstraction. For players that want to do more manual exploration, we’ve added options to remove the sense cues for optional collectibles, and one to make scent trails dimmer until the player requests a hint.

Ultimately, enhanced senses are still essential to creating an authentic Wolverine, and that’s still reflected in the cinematic and environmental storytelling of the game. I think it’s great that on top of that, players now have more flexibility in how they experience them.

As a longtime comics fan, I found Logan’s combat system especially exciting, particularly for the relentless forward momentum it provided. What do you think were some of the keys to nailing that dynamic, as distinct from other high-quality third-person action games?

There were a few key elements we wanted to get right - Logan’s resilience, rage, claw feel, and overall lethality.

For resilience, Logan’s healing factor needed to feel important for survival - a prominent element of the system. A natural starting point there was to try continual regeneration so you could outlast enemies, but that quickly fell apart as it incentivized the player to slow the pace of combat or even retreat for maximum advantage. Even though it was incredibly effective at enabling survival, it was also hard to notice by the player so it didn’t feel prominent.

The key to solving this problem was making a connection between rage and healing factor. The Last Stand mechanic is a healing surge that can happen when you lose all your health, themed as using adrenaline to keep Logan’s heart beating. This incentivized aggression and made a space for an up-close look at visceral healing.

Speaking of rage, it’s the backbone of the combat system where being an indicator of momentum is key. At the low end of rage, you don’t have the safety net of Last Stand, so your decision-making naturally biases towards survival; ensuring you prioritize threat assessment and defense. As you climb into the middle tier, you have the leeway to push your luck for longer combos or barrages that let you build up rage and get kills faster. Finally, you get to rage tier 3, where the quick decay of rage makes your rate of kills the top priority, so you might prefer to attack groups over ranged stragglers just for the improved kill density. Beyond the mechanics, we change the presentation of combat, especially through Logan’s animations and exertion to reflect his state of mind. The presentation and systemic incentives drive the player into a frenzy, just like Wolverine.

We invested a lot in the details of claw feel to make sure it was distinct from general game attacks. Claws shred, so we added locational body damage to our enemies to reflect that, along with a dynamic blood system where it globs together as it is spilled, splatters on contact with characters or the environment, drips down the walls, diffuses in the water, and other details. Many kills throughout combat are punctuated with custom animations with cinematic camera work that pushes in and frames the puncturing of claws into the body for a strong impression of the connection and weight of the puncture. Severing limbs on these attacks is an occasional reminder of how sharp Logan’s adamantium claws are. Reinforcing this is top-notch sound and haptics design, so each hit registers.

The last aspect I’ll touch on is lethality, the rate at which Wolverine is able to dispatch enemies and vice versa. We found that fights where enemies were more technical and could survive a lot undermined what players expected to experience as Wolverine, which was aggressively and lethally tearing through a lot of enemies. On the other hand, combat was less exciting if the enemies didn’t feel like a serious and deadly threat, and you didn’t feel like Wolverine if a little bit of caution could enable you to defend perfectly and avoid all damage.

These aspects led us towards encounters where you confronted large groups of enemies that were highly aggressive, to the point of feeling unfair. Enemies can’t believably go toe-to-toe with Wolverine alone, even world-class mercenaries, so their strategy is in group coordination, which creates a counterweight to Wolverine’s own rage-based momentum.

Marvel’s Wolverine draws in a number of characters from across the X-Men comic mythology, but notably makes no mention of some foundational figures of that fiction – Professor Xavier and Magneto. That, in turn, leads to dramatically different lives for characters like Jean Grey or Logan. Is the narrative you crafted an intentional exploration of a world where those figures weren’t present in the early days of mutant emergence?

I would say it was more of an exploration of the character than the world. We wanted a story where Logan is pulled into conflict not because he’s a crusader, but because there’s no other option. There are no X-Men to help. His growth as a person should be a challenging journey, which could go unearned if he was surrounded by wise, supportive, heroic characters pushing him in the right direction. In contrast, his dynamic with the members of Team X evokes his struggle. The adversity to personal growth is what makes it interesting.

Jean does end up being the person that pushes him in the right direction, and that works because they can relate to each other, having had similar struggles.

In several versions of Marvel storytelling, Jean and Logan share a special bond, but Jean ultimately chooses Scott Summers as a partner. But even without that barrier in your story, Logan still hits some roadblocks to love. Is Wolverine fundamentally a better character when he just can’t get the girl?

The way I would put it is that a Wolverine story is fundamentally better when you empathize with Logan’s pain and admire him for pressing on despite it. That goes for his emotional pain as much as physical. He’s a tragic character in this regard – all he wants is to be at peace but can never find it for long.

Wolverine gets to take on a lot of the “heavy hitters” of his comic mythology in different boss fights throughout the game. When you began development, do you recall who the very first character was that you decided he simply had to fight in your game?

Sabretooth. No character is a better foil for Logan. His inner turmoil and chaotic behavior helps illustrate Logan’s own inner beast and his struggle to resist it. Sabretooth’s strength and mutant powers also provide a mirror to Logan in combat, and his savagery creates shocking moments that leave an impression. We knew an epic confrontation with Sabretooth was going to be a thing from the start.

#4267. Here's Our Ranking Of Every MTG Set Released This Year

Another year has come and gone for Magic: The Gathering, at least from a set perspective, with seven total releases from Lorywn Eclipsed up to Star Trek. Not all sets are created equal, and fan reaction has ranged from jubilation to disdain, but each set has had positives; the question is whether the negatives outweighed them.

Our ranking considers each release's full product lineup, fan reception, draftability and impact across formats, and, finally, the set's mechanical and artistic design. With that tidied up, here are our Magic: The Gathering set rankings for 2026 as we now turn our attention to what's to come from Magic in 2027.

Starting with what Star Trek gets right, it's a fun set to draft, and even if you don't have a deep understanding of the lore and universe, the mechanics are fairly sound and do come across like an EOE 2, if that helps. The prerelease experience was good for us, and attendance didn't noticeably dip, although reports from around the world suggest otherwise.The Commander precon decks for Star Trek are pretty good, with We Are The Borg among the better decks released this year, as is Landing Party, though the remaining two decks are a little unremarkable without considerable upgrades.

The first thing Star Trek gets hugely wrong is its stock availability and its proximity to Reality Fracture. This set shouldn't have been released just six weeks after a capstone set that ended the years-long story arc for in-universe lore. On top of that, product availability was at its worst for this set, and while every set has had some sort of problem this year, every Star Trek product has had confirmed issues in some regions, and the Beginner Box was even canceled because things got so bad.Thematically, the art and lore behind Star Trek just don't mesh as well as many other Universes Beyond sets. This issue will come up again for a set released this year, but it came as a slight shock to us, given we actually thought EOE paved the way for Star Trek to feel at home in the Magic universe. Alas, this wasn't the case, and criticisms of the art are well-founded, not because it isn't high quality and gorgeous to look at, but because it isn't what we've come to expect from Magic artwork.Finally, outside the draft experience, very few cards look set to make a big impact in formats like Standard, Commander, or Modern. Time may change that, but for now, it doesn't look promising.

The Universes Beyond sets are often extremely divisive, but some are much better than others, so we've ranked every one so far.

While it won't be winning any awards for being the most powerful or outright best Commander precon of the year, the Heroes in a Half Shell deck tried something different and told a thematic story within itself, and in truth had more effort put into it than the rest of the set combined, from a lore standpoint. This makes it super fun to play with, and we're happy to leave it untouched as a result.This is also another fun drafting set, and while our prerelease experience wasn't quite as fun because of poor local attendance, we've since enjoyed a lot of drafting via MTG Arena instead.Finally, Turtle Team-Up was a great idea for a new product to focus on co-op play as a way to get new players into Magic, and everything in this kit could then be used to get a new player into the one-vs-one version of the game, too.

Pretty much everything else about TMNT was bad. Its impact on the game and across formats has been minimal. Art-wise, so many of the cards are once again just character portraits, and while that may suit fans of the property, it isn't good enough for Magic. On top of this, the Kevin Eastman-signed headliner cards felt like a cash grab to push collector booster boxes.TMNT should be used as the poster child for why animated kids' shows should stick to Secret Lair drops and not become the centerpiece of an entire Magic set.

All four Marvel Super Heroes Commander precons are pretty solid, both out of the box and with some upgrades. We're particularly big fans of Avengers Assemble and Doom Previews.The collectibility of this set is a positive, with certain card art styles being very eye-catching, and the continuation of the Infinity Stones slowly releasing in MTG means the set carried a high initial value, which was good for players who were looking to buy product early and ditch their "valuable" cards to keep the essentials they needed or wanted for projects.

This set truly started the debate about legendary creatures and the insane number of them in Universes Beyond sets. As a result, the sets' draftability suffered, and their fairly weak archetypes didn't help either.While some Marvel cards have penetrated other formats, like Hawkeye's Bow, some went too far, like Fantasticar, and required an immediate ban.Scalping and the general value of sealed products were also issues, which created a bubble of sorts. For example, Draft Night bundles were hard to find at MSRP in a few stores we visited around launch, yet barely two months later at MagicCon Amsterdam, they were selling for almost half MSRP as retailers tried to offload stock.Finally, for a property with so many well-known household names, there were simply too many big names missing from the set, and lesser-known characters made up quite a large portion of the card, which then let players know that their favorite characters are likely coming in future sets, or have arrived in one of the 10 or so Secret Lair bundles that have dropped since Marvel Super Heroes launched.

The lead-up to the launch of Lorwyn Eclipsed also set a new standard for how in-universe sets are handled now compared to Universes Beyond, and we're big fans of the approach.

Lorwyn Eclipsed has a great draft experience and prerelease window, and while the failure of Spider-Man would have helped this, Lorwyn still had to show up and get the job done, and it did.Both of Lorwyn's Commander precons are solid, but we'd argue Dance of the Elements is one of the stronger precons in recent memory when you fully understand what the deck is trying to achieve and the benefit of Ashling, the Limitless' Evoke ability.The card art is fantastic, although it does still sit behind every set that outranks it, but it's light-years better than the three preceding it. Lore-wise, the story is strong, but it would have been a little better tied into the overarching story of Jace, the Multiverse, and where we would eventually end up come Reality Fracture. By this, we mean that much of the flavor and lore was delivered outside the set, rather than directly through the cards.Finally, Lorwyn Eclipsed introduced the Draft Night product, which has become a staple for all releases and remains a great value for groups of four who want to run a draft and give the winner a prize.

Lorwyn's long-term viability is poor, and by the end of 2026, its impact on Standard in particular felt quite limited, although a few cards are still hanging on as part of some popular meta decks. The upcoming Standard rotation could change this, though.The booster fun side of the card design is a little boring, and while there are some nice cards, the forced introduction of a serialized chase card is a bit nauseating, and it felt like there was no real freedom with some of the variants; i.e., the Japanese fractured foils didn't really fit the feel of the set, so why were they included?

We're in the back end of 2026, and with five of the seven MTG sets now out, we're going to rank all the Commander precons we've seen so far.

The Hobbit is up there as one of our favorite drafting experiences yet, and the set's smaller size played a big role. This also explains why we didn't like other aspects of the set, but it really worked for the Limited format and made for a brilliant prerelease.Art in this set is incredible, and fits both the Magic and Tolkien feel perfectly, which isn't often the case with Universes Beyond sets.This set also beefed up some exciting creature types like Dwarves, Goblins, and Dragons, making it fun to build decks exclusively from the set while also benefiting decks across a bunch of formats, especially Commander.The product lineup for The Hobbit was great, with the Scene Boxes being among the first of their kind to be worth collecting.Finally, this set opened the door for the return of some very powerful reprints, with Mox Amber among the Eternal cards released in the set. While not confirmed, this feels like a test run for future Mox cards and other iconic Vintage cards to return as reprints, which would hopefully bring market prices down and make them easier to collect overall.

The Hobbit is a smaller Standard set, which made it feel light on cards and didn't really give it a chance to have much impact on Standard or Commander, despite the size being a plus for drafting.We didn't need a gold, numbered Smaug card, and the controversy this card ended up causing with prices and sales just proves that serialized products don't belong anywhere near Magic: The Gathering.

Secrets of Strixhaven is one of the best sets for lore in recent years, with the surprise drop of "Off the Record" which kickstarted the intrigue over what Reality Fracture would eventually become, and this strong storytelling continued not only in the podcast episodes but into the cards themselves. This is supported by truly phenomenal art throughout the set, with no card looking out of place, and it is a set well worth collecting for art alone.The draft experience was utterly brilliant thanks to the decision to include the Strixhaven College seeded pack in each kit, meaning you already had some direction regarding your draft deck, but a downside to this is that you often couldn't guarantee you would get your chosen college if you did have a preference.When it comes to bonus sheets, the Mystical Archive is our favorite, and it returned even better this time around, with the Japanese and Silver Scroll variants making for some huge chase cards that can freshen up decks across Eternal formats.Card variants across the board felt better suited to Strixhaven and didn't default to forced template designs. Each variant, from the field notes to the borderless showcase cards, all tied in perfectly with the feel of the set.We got a Commander precon for each of the Strixhaven Colleges, and none of them were bad. Each one leaned into a unique Magic strategy, and the prices made them easy to collect without breaking the bank. Better still, if you like to upgrade precons, these decks made it easy to raise the power level, but they were great for casual play right out of the box.

If we're being extremely nitpicky, the introduction of the Codex Bundle has triggered a ripple effect of in-universe sets, now including a limited, premium bundle that feels unnecessary. OG gift bundles are still used for Universes Beyond, so either adopt these back into in-universe sets, or don't bother, but don't start releasing more limited products that are just going to be the target of scalpers.

Everything.No, really, everything about Reality Fracture delivered in a way that only a capstone Magic set can. Everything felt important, everything felt meaningful, and when we finally got our hands on the cards, the gameplay experience was unmatched in the year of 2026.From the incredible drafting experience, which was enhanced by the Echoed Pairs mechanic, which could see normal Play Boosters pop off with some big cards, or just the playability of the set in the Limited format, it was easily up there as one of the best prerelease events ever.While the lore leading up to Reality Fracture was stellar, the story of the set itself tied everything together beautifully, and while Jace may no longer be around to terrorize the Multiverse, we're left with so many exciting story threads that still need to be tied up as we move into the next phase of the Magic universe.Art in the set is perfect again, but we especially have to call out the Shattered Mirror cards and the borderless showcase Planeswalkers, which can be brought together to create complete works of art while still working incredibly well as standalone cards.Gameplay-wise, many cards have gone straight into Standard meta decks, and Commander also got a huge dump of exciting new cards to play with, many of which came in the single precon that launched with the set.Overall, Reality Fracture just had everything you could possibly want from an in-universe Magic set, and now Wizards of the Coast has the monumental task of following that up with Nauctis early next year.

For the sake of fairness, the Secret Lair bundle was this set's Codex Bundle, and it was very poorly handled despite some cool exclusive card art, so that can't be ignored.

We want to hear from you. Share your perspective in the comments below, and please keep the conversation respectful.

#4266. You're not crazy, trying to heal in Nioh 3 sometimes doesn't work - and Team Ninja is fixing it

One of the more insidiously aggravating bugs in Nioh 3 makes it so the game ignores you when you try to use elixirs, but hopefully not for long.

Nioh 3 has received a hot new update that brings plenty of bug fixes to very specific issues, but it also implements fixes for a few of the most common - and incredibly annoying - bugs. Patch 1.03.01 arrived earlier on all platforms, and it comes with a chunky set of notes.

This latest update, predictably, doesn’t add any gameplay features, but some of the included fixes will absolutely delight - or vindicate - so many of the game’s millions of players.

There’s plenty to go through in the patch notes published today for update 1.03.01, but the most impactful is a fix for an issue that “sometimes made it impossible to use elixirs during battle.” This is only a partial fix, but if you ran into the problem of smashing that shortcut button and not seeing your character play the healing animation, you’ll be glad to see it.

This is a problem myself and others have faced, especially in boss fights. You can even see the shortcut register your button press and proceed to ignore you. Another partial fix has been made to an issue that caused the game to crash. Team Ninja didn’t share specifics on that, and though Nioh 3 has been fairly stable for me in 70+ hours, it has definitely crashed a few times.

If you’ve been playing since launch, you likely have - or know someone who has - run into issues with save file corruption and other weird bugs around certain trackable items within save files.

Team Ninja already rolled out a couple of fixes there, and this latest one specifically targets losing valuables during Myths. If your save file has been affected, the game will now check and recover what was lost. Even more interesting is that the game will now automatically create a backup copy of your save data any time you load a save.

If you’ve made it into the Eternal Rift, you’ll be happy to know that today’s update takes care of a few progression blockers, and fixes an issue that allowed some players to obtain certain items before they were supposed to, locking themselves out.

One of the more amusing fixes concerns Mujina, who had a tendency to respawn if you prayed at a Shrine after opening a chest it was hiding in, which made it appear far more often than a mimic should.

Finally, there’s a set of fixes that address bugs (and exploits) when using specific Martial Art with certain weapons. There are a few fixes to AI, Myths, and one problem with the Minamoto no Yoritomo boss fight that made it impossible to interrupt him, even after he runs out of Ki.

Hit the link at the top for the full change log, and check out our Nioh 3 gameplay tips if you haven’t already. You should also change these settings ASAP, as they’re going to make your life much easier and save you a lot of time.

#4265. Hillthorn, the card-based detective sim, is out now on iOS and Android

Even if Halloween is done and dusted, the November nights are drawing in, making it perfect for something spooky to play. And if that's the mood that's taking you, then publisher Raw Fury and developer Fool Moon's latest release that's just landed for iOS and Android, Hillthorn, should be more than enough in the way of chills and thrills.

Hillthorn is a card-based detective sim, where you take on the role of investigating a mysterious community and the case of a disappeared child. With time in short supply, and the maze-like trails of Hillthorn Mountain threatening to swallow you whole (perhaps literally), there's not long to find out whodunnit and why.

There's undoubtedly a bit of a gimmick-y element to it, but Hillthorn isn't exactly selling itself on an original story here. A spooky town, missing child and possible cult are elements as old as the horror genre itself, but it's the way they're executed that will decide whether you're enticed to give Hillthorn a go.

Personally, I can very much see myself enjoying Hillthorn. The atmosphere and the mysterious, detached nature of the setting, thanks to the cards, mean you're challenged to make some truly devious deductions. And all the while, new cards offer fresh routes to pursue, although some may be more deadly than others...

And if Hillthorn isn't enough in the way of chills and thrills to satisfy you, then don't worry. Because our list of the best horror games on Android is truly evergreen, no matter what time of the year it may be!

#4264. Holiday Gift Guide 2026

With the holiday gift-giving season upon us, it’s time to think about the gaming fans in your life and find the ideal present to brighten their day. And if you’re the gamer in the family, we always encourage you to circle relevant items in the coming pages and leave your magazine open in hard-to-miss locations around the house. We’ve scoured dozens of tech products, tabletop games, collectibles, and more to select and highlight some of the coolest items we found this year.

We recommended the Board shortly after its launch, but with its expanded game library and lower price than first-adopter rates, this holiday season is an ideal time to make the leap. This family-friendly platform features original games that sit comfortably between the digital and physical divide. The horizontally placed screen shows the backdrop of one of the several included games, or the sold-separately add-on games that have popped in since launch. Each game has its own real physical play pieces that interact with the action onscreen, often in innovative and charming ways. Think of it as the best of both worlds between board games and video games, and you’ll get what they’re shooting for here. $399

Few additions to the latest Dungeons & Dragons rules pack as much punch and value as this new expansion, focusing on ways to develop further and evolve the use of magic across your tabletop gaming sessions. New subclasses, spells, creatures, magical items, and factions add thoughtful, intriguing options for both players looking to play someone new and DMs hunting for new story hooks and challenges. $50

If you’re as excited as we are about this month’s celebration of the Tomb Raider legacy (see p. 40), this centerpiece statue is an ideal fit for your collection. Standing roughly nine inches in height, Lara is poised for exploration in her original classic garb. The sculpt strikes a perfect balance between crisp detail and stylistic presentation, in line with that early version of the character; the metallic blue motorcycle paint is especially striking. $250

For players longing for the glory days of stand-up arcade games, it’s hard to beat Arcade 1Up’s approach. The team’s sturdy cabinets look and sound great as a marquee feature of your game room. The new Outrun machine features much of the original display art, a bright 19-inch screen, and responsive gas and brake pedals as you steer around those tight corners. Sega has packed in OutRun, Turbo OutRun, OutRunners, and Power Drift. If old-school racing isn’t your thing, look for cabinets that run the gamut from Pac-Man to Joust to Claw Machines. $629.99

The long-running Nendoroid figures continue to be an attractive but still affordable choice for building collections across numerous fan-favorite series. There are somewhere around 2000 characters at this point! New entries like the Genshin Impact collection make a strong case for the line. The look is chibi, the quality is excellent, poseability is high, and customizable face and accessory parts let you change up your display over time. $46

We’ve previously sung the praises of Libernovo’s versatile approach to an ergonomic gaming chair, which includes a lumbar stretch functionality, a steady recline option for comfortable pushback without sudden shifts, and dynamically adjusting parts as you move through your day. The Maxis line does all that, but addresses one of the fundamental problems for at least some users with the original – it wasn’t big enough. With features like a wider base and longer headrest reach, the Maxis aims to provide the same comfort to the players who are tall or wide enough to need the extra breathing room. $1119

If you’re the player on your team who likes to have easy access to soundboards and real-time voice changing, the Key Pocket could be just the ticket. This small device straps onto your phone for mobile play, but it’s also compatible with consoles, Discord, Twitch, or just about any place you want to tweak audio on the fly. A free tier gives you access to some voice-changing and sounds, while a separate subscription opens up hundreds of thousands of additional options. But be warned: we can’t help you after your friends abandon you for that baby voice you won’t stop using. $99

The question of the best bang for your buck in modern consoles has become extraordinarily complicated, especially as tech prices have soared in recent years. There’s no right answer, but Sony’s high-end machine walks the line of offering extremely high-tier performance without escalating to even higher-priced gaming PCs. Higher and more consistent frame rates than on standard PS5, advanced ray tracing, and an increasing number of games that feature enhanced PSSR image options all add up to a better gaming experience, if you’re ready to make the significant price jump. $900

If the gamer in your life is looking for a stylish, understated way to express their love of the hobby, Anicorn’s designer watch collaboration with PlayStation could be a standout option. Available in black and a slick silver/white combo, the minimalist timepiece includes the familiar face buttons of Sony’s controller encased in an oil-injection display so they slowly and freely float across the watch as you move. $250

It’s a safe bet you’ve at least seen the popular Shashibo puzzle cubes by this point. We’ve been fans of their brain-teasing, fidgety fun for some time. Battle Shapes takes the core concept – reshaping the box into various distinct magnetically-locked shapes – and extends it into a timed game experience, playable solo or head-to-head. By targeting specific shapes, you significantly improve your speed with the toy, and scannable QR codes on the cards offer clear tutorials for each shape so you can prep for competition. $50

While the vast majority of gamers looking for good personal audio are going to be okay with a larger set of cans over their ears, We know more than a few players for whom that’s a definite no – for comfort, awareness of surrounding sounds, or other reasons. The Arc 5 earbuds aim to solve for that, with an over-ear design that feels extremely comfortable. And because they sit on the ear, you can still hear what’s going on around you. While that limits some aspects of the final sound quality, the inclusion of THX certification, Dolby Atmos optimization, and Dynamic Bass Enhancement helps to ensure audio is still very strong. $230

Across Lego’s many recent themes, Tolkien’s legendarium has offered some stellar sets. The largest yet is the capital of Gondor, with an astonishing 8,278 pieces and a height of roughly two feet. The castle/city build is impressive, featuring tons of interesting angles and turns. The finished product aims to offer the best of both worlds in presentation – a microscale representation of the front façade and a reverse minifigure-scale Hall of Kings. We especially like the inclusion of Denethor’s cherry tomatoes. $650

The original Azul is often cited as a foundational entry in modern board gaming. The “Kids” versions of celebrated titles aren’t always a sure bet, but this one holds up to scrutiny. Azul Kids lowers the complexity threshold but keeps the foundational strategic thinking. Players lay out uniquely shaped tiles into mosaic frameworks in colorful, appealing patterns; the basic concept of the original inspiration is clear, and kids as young as five can grasp and enjoy the fun. $25

Many corners of the collecting world have embraced the fun (and frequent despair) of blind boxes, where you never know exactly who you’ll get in a given series. Funism has a strong track record for quality, offering adorable smaller figures like their latest line of Evangelion collectibles. Each figure stands nearly four inches and features both human characters and mecha. You can buy singles and roll the dice, or purchase larger sets with a no-duplicates guarantee, which can save a lot of heartache if you’re trying to line your whole shelf. $21

If you’re going to spring for a high-end keyboard for PC gaming, it’s important that you like the feel of the keys. The slightly smaller overall 75% size profile of this Blackwidow has no impact on the great feel of typing – a clear highlight for the unit. The customizable, colored backlights are also a big selling point, as is the side command dial and built-in OLED display, which can be tweaked to show PC performance, GIFs, lighting brightness, and more. It’s a strong contender in a crowded field, and justifies its price with both comfort and customizability. $300

Beautiful, vibrant art and a refreshing take on the classic area-control board game genre are the two strongest reasons to take a close look at Wroth. Players control one of five races vying for supremacy across a conflict-ridden peninsula. Factions are asymmetric, so everyone has unique capabilities, and that adds significant replayability. Players roll and draft dice, allowing distinct actions that move the game forward. And move it does; unlike many games of this ilk, Wroth can be learned quickly and played to completion in a little over an hour. $65

Console and computer hardware prices are skyrocketing with no sign of slowing, and perhaps as a result, retro gaming handhelds are gaining popularity. Many quality devices are available, but what sets the Evercade Nexus apart is its officially licensed game cartridges. Imagine the nostalgic joy of a Game Boy, but with a cartridge that includes both Banjo-Kazooie and Tooie. The cartridge boxes even include manuals. For fans of physical media, Evercade Nexus is a great option. $199

This tiny USB-C plug-in (with included USB-A adapter) solves a bunch of audio challenges in one uniform device. It offers high-resolution Bluetooth transmission on iPhone, high-bitrate audio transmission to compatible LDAC headphones, enables high-quality Bluetooth output from your PC, and even low-latency Bluetooth audio on PS5 and Switch. In short, it takes a huge number of products with a USB port and ensures a dynamic Bluetooth audio connection with relative ease. $99

The original MV6 is a familiar sight on streams thanks to its clear voice reproduction and overall ease of use. Shure has built on that success with the Gen 2, offering an excellent standalone mic that doesn’t break the bank. Available in black or white, the Gen 2 features a handy auto-level mode that keeps volume even as you adjust your own amplitude, an adjustable denoiser for your space, a longer cable for out-of-the-box convenience, and three presets for plug-and-play use. In short, it’s an excellent choice if you want great performance without needing an audio engineering degree. $169

XR Glasses are still fighting for awareness, but once you try them, it’s easy to see why the concept is on the rise. Viture’s Pro 2 makes an impressive case for adoption, with a competitive price point, comfortable wear, and a giant 146-inch screen that floats in front of your face for gaming or work on your PC or phone. The display is crisp, bright, and impressive, even as the glasses are light and easy to use. With a mobile dock mini (sold separately), you can even snap onto a Switch 2 with ease and start playing instantly. $299

Role-playing gamers have several excellent universal systems to pick between when considering a story or campaign idea that might fall outside traditional genre staples. Among many good options, Cypher stands out as one of the very best. The system uses a rules-light, narrative-focused approach that prioritizes player-driven storytelling across everything from hard sci-fi to superheroes to intrigue- driven espionage. This is the corebook that’s needed to run and play the full system; additional books only add options. $50

As gamers have continually migrated toward personal audio that can rock amazing sound without disturbing the whole house, high-end premium headphones have become a dangerously competitive space. Turtle Beach meets that challenge head-on, with a robust option that sounds beautiful in use. The Stealth Pro II boasts the slick ability to wirelessly switch between different devices, which is awesome if you’re one of those players who regularly jumps between platforms to play your favorite titles. Like the whole category, it’s a lot to spend on a headset, but Dolby Atmos, active noise cancellation, and 60mm dual drivers all add up to a powerful argument. $300

With an increasing number of top-tier console and PC games like Resident Evil Village, No Man’s Sky, and Dead Cells now available on iOS, not to mention the consistent quality of Apple Arcade, Apple phones remain the best mobile platform for gaming. The 18 Pro Max phone has implemented a number of tweaks that strengthen the platform, including higher memory, much faster graphics processing, impressive HDR performance, and notably improved battery life, all adding up to a gaming experience that is working hard to justify your playtime when away from home. Starting at $1299

SteelSeries is best known for its strong audio line-up, but its push into premium-tier controllers exhibits a similar flair for quality and usability. The new Aeon Pro has a lot to recommend it as your go-to Xbox, PC, or mobile choice. The two included batteries (one of which can always be charging in the dock) ensure essentially unlimited playtime. The full-pull or hair triggers and buttons are clicky and satisfying, and the Hall Effect thumbsticks are built to minimize any drift. Textured handgrips and overall heft are ideal. And an onboard OLED lets you adjust profiles and button assignments, switch between platforms, and check battery at a glance. $260

Valve’s pricey VR headset isn’t a revolution in the medium, but the company has been invested in the technology since its inception. As a result, the Steam Frame is a very good, very comfortable headset. Like its competition, the Quest, its best use is playing games locally on the headset, and Steam’s library is vast and interesting. Wireless connected play to a powerful PC is also well done, but currently the included Wireless Adapter is not fully compatible with the Steam Machine – a baffling limitation we were shocked to confirm. VR is an expensive sub-hobby within video games, but Steam Frame is among the best ways to explore and enjoy it. $1059

Many of the coolest “gaming lights” focus on the flexibility and fun of bright RGB customization. While we’re fans of that aesthetic, it leaves others out in the cold who might want something a bit more natural. The Elements hex panels feature a natural wood-inspired panel, customizable “scenes” like a campfire glow, and can react to both music and touch, with adjustable ambient white light to keep the vibe relaxed. $200

Kyle Hilliard contributed to this article.
