#4223. Murals Interview: How To Create A Mascot Who's Not As Annoying As Ocarina Of Time's Navi

Scott Baird is a Contributor from the UK with over a decade of video game writing experience.

Murals is an upcoming action RPG by Dlala Studios that, on the surface, looks a great deal like Hades. The concept of Murals involves twisted and humorous takes on classic fairy tales, like Rapunzel, which is an idea that’s more commonplace than the straight tellings of those stories, with everyone from Disney to Alan Moore turning fables on their head.

Originality isn’t the golden ticket to a video game being enjoyable, and in this case, the differences from genre norms are in the gameplay, not the story. While Murals might look like countless isometric action RPG roguelikes on Steam, it’s going for a linear, narrative-based progression, with crafted levels and enemies, rather than relying on randomness.

Playing it straight is a surprisingly bold move, and it runs counter to the story of Murals. DualShockers recently visited Dlala’s offices to preview Murals, where we got the chance to speak to the studio’s CEO, AJ Grand-Scrutton, about the many choices that went into making Murals.

Q: The idea of fables and fairy tales being twisted and viewed through a modern lens has been done many times before. Were there any specific examples that inspired Murals?

Grand-Scrutton: So obviously the source material was where we went to initially, the grim stuff and the Hans Christian Andersen. But I mean, I loved American McGee's Alice. I was a massive fan of that. There's a lot of like comic books as well, like Fables. I love Wolf Among Us. So I love that familiarity that you recognize the story, but enough difference that you don't feel you're just retreading old ground.

Q: Have any video games inspired the gameplay or design of Murals?

Grand-Scrutton: Obviously, Murals is isometric and it's got pretty chaotic moment to moment. So a lot of modern Roguelikes, your Hades, et cetera. I struggle with permadeath, especially as I've got older. I'm quite impatient and moody. And so kind of what I really loved was like the moment to moment in a lot of modern roguelikes, but I didn't necessarily get on very well with the permadeath loop. So that was a big influence for how murals came about.

Like, can we take some of those chaotic moment to moment experiences; those combat augmentation systems and deliver them in like a bit longer form content? And also like, you know, weird influences in there as well. You know, like a lot of our world building Psychonauts and a lot of double fine stuff was really prominent in our minds. And, you know, classic combat games like DMC, Bayonetta.

But yeah, it was really just about us trying to capture an experience we didn't feel we could fully play out there already.

We traveled to China to chat with Soulframe about his upcoming action RPG, Phantom Blade Zero.

Q: The protagonist is mostly silent in Murals, with most of the talking being done by the character’s sidekick, Loaf. How do you go about designing a talkative side character like Loaf in a way that makes them likeable. Were there any concerns they’d become another Navi from Ocarina of Time?

Grand-Scrutton: Yeah, so, I mean, we always are very aware that our style of writing can become... Every character can feel like that very quickly for people. I mean, I think if you look at Battletoads, you look at Illusion Island and you look at Murals, you can tell it's very much like the same writing team that have done them.

Loaf is kind of, in a weird way, is obviously this sentient sketch come to life. He's the most naturally written character because it's often me and Kelsey, my lead writer, just typing what we're thinking about situations or stupid commets. Like, often we'll just be on calls and we'll play through the game. And Kelsey, as well as writing, she actually is Loaf. She does the voice of Loaf. And we'll almost do our own little director's commentaries as we're playing the game to figure out where Loaf comments should go and what would Loaf say in this situation.

I think with humour, comedy in games, we're not unique. There's other people that do comedy games, but it's still quite a niche. And I think you kind of just have to lean into what you are. And I think that we are that self-referential type of humour. We do the fourth wall breaking. There is the modern label of the meta-level stuff in there. And I think it'd be easy for us to go half-arsed or half-cocked on it. But we just kind of leant into it. This is what we find funny, and that's kind of how we write the game.

Q: Why go for such a basic, sketch outline design for Loaf?

Grand-Scrutton: Yeah, I love the juxtaposition. So obviously, as you've seen from the couple of murals you've played, the characters that live in the world are hand-animated, but they've still got depth to them.

The invasive forces, which is the distorted, the enemies, and the hero, the player, are fully animated. And I love this idea that Loaf was just... the hero just made this rough sketch in their notebook or something and accidentally got brought to life. I love Doodlebob, who is definitely an influence from the SpongeBob cartoons.

I just think there's something really nice about... we've got these animated characters that are still not realistic, but almost like they make sense. And then Loaf is just a cartoon. He doesn't really have the rules of physicality that a humanoid would have. He is just who he is. And I think that just gave us some really fun opportunities, and it let us do some silly things with him.

An interview with Jonathan Blow about the making and future of Order of the Sinking Star.

Q: Is Murals intended as a linear experience, or is there more of a roguelike/Hades-style progression, with a hub area, random layouts, and upgrades sticking between runs.

Grand-Scrutton: No, it's very, very linear. Like, we're always up front about that because we know how misleading it can be when you see like an isometric action game. It's very linear. Like, the only real elements of random to it are the order you get the areas in.

So, you know, if you do a playthrough, you may get different areas to someone else doing the exact same playthrough. But the story, the quests, the enemies themselves, that is all very sculpted.

Q: In the Murals preview, there’s a very generous window for being able to dash out of attacks. Is this planned to be maintained for the final build or is the gameplay balance being tweaked still, out of fear it could make the combat too easy?

Grand-Scrutton: Yes, no, maybe to all the above. We're still tweaking. We'll be tweaking until my Tech Director pries it from my cold dead hands. We definitely have gone generous with a lot of things like this. I think the difficulty you're playing in general is probably on the easier side of what we would balance the final game.

You know, we're looking to make it customizable though, right? In terms of like enemy health, enemy damage, amount of health, you probably notice in the build you're playing right now that you always have enough health drops to get full health basically. That would probably be the generous setting on the slider for health drops. But I think the dash serves a very specific purpose in our game, obviously it's not unique at all.

But we've got a lot of boss fights, environmental hazards and other enemies as you progress through the game where giving the players a generous dash meant we could get more chaotic with the experience. I think, you know, if you look at our game and compare to some of our other peers, I think that's one of the slight difference of our moment to moment.

I think we're not a one versus one experience. We're not one versus many. We're like a one versus some is what I like to say. But we do reasonably small spaces with a reasonably large amount of enemies. And so while the play space is quite chaotic, we wanted to give the player simple enough verbs that they could control so they never felt like the game was being unfair.

DualShockers spoke with the developers of Wo Long 2: Wings of Ember about why a sequel was made and how the gameplay has changed from its predecessor.

Q: Some of the enemies have a flashing light before they attacked. Is this hinting at a parry mechanic for the full version of the game? Do you dare release a game in 2027 with no parrying?

Grand-Scrutton: I mean, we are daring to not release. No, there's no parry. They're very generous tells on some of the enemies that do more damage. We definitely discussed parrying really early on. We discussed parrying, we discussed blocking. But it just, it felt a bit like a hat on a hat for what we were making. Like, you know, we like, we believe in like, depth through simplicity. This is not a big combo based game.

You know, it's not even as combo laden as like our Battletoads was. It's a very simple amount of inputs with like varying weapons and a lot of depth comes through the power-ups. And the problem I find with parrying is like, modern games are amazing.

Like, you know, Expedition 33, all these games are absolutely outstanding. I find when I play them that my gameplay just becomes around parrying. All I do is parry. Like, in a lot of ways, although I love them, I play them multiple times.

I felt that learning to do the block timing in the Arkham games made the combat a little bit less exciting for me because I actually certainly changed my entire strategy in those games to be let the enemy come to me. And I just didn't want that for this. I didn't want the focus to be on parry timing. I wanted the focus to just be like, have a little bit of fun controlled chaos.

Q: Finally, why choose Murals as the game’s name?

Grand-Scrutton: Yeah, we are traditionally, not necessarily publicly, very awful at doing project codenames. Like, the codename for Battletoads was Frogspawn, which is not the most... And the codename for Illusion Island was Illusions because we weren't originally going to call it that.

So Project Murals was the codename for Murals because we love the idea that these worlds are like these fairy tales brought to life by through these painted murals the creator has done. But the team will tell you, I have this obsession, I think Pokémon is the greatest name for a franchise ever because I love a name that is memorable and it's also the name of a thing in the game or in the world. And I love the idea of us having murals because the levels are called murals and it's also the name and it makes sense.

So it's kind of like this dragon I've been chasing and it just fit the game and it worked for me. And there's some funniness in there as well to me through some previous titles we've worked on and stuff in the past where we've tried to put forward names for things and we've been told that the majority of the...

We had a game we were working on years ago, years and years ago, and it was around animatronics. And this was years back. I mean, it was before it was necessarily common lingo but I really wanted to call it Tronics and I was like, oh, how cool is this name? And we got told by our partners at the time that no one knows what an animatronic is so we couldn't do it. And then Five Nights at Freddy's came out a year later and I was like, everyone knows what animatronic is, look.

And we've had similar things with this, like when we'd kind of pitched this to people before the name Murals, people were like, I don't think anyone's gonna really know what a mural is. And I was like, I'm pretty sure people know what a mural is. So it was nice to kind of have that control ourselves.

#4222. GTA 6 Is Now The Most Pre-Ordered Game Ever

It was always safe to assume that GTA 6 would sell millions of copies before release day thanks to excited fans of the series placing pre-orders. Now we have data not only confirming exactly that, but also that GTA 6 has become the most pre-ordered game ever with nine days still to go.

That's according to the latest data shared by Sensor Tower. According to the data analysis site, GTA 6 has been pre-ordered 9.69 million times so far across PS5 and Xbox Series X|S. That will net Rockstar and Take-Two Interactive almost $1 billion in revenue before anyone has even played the game, and means Cyberpunk 2077's long-standing record has been broken.

One game occupying all three medal positions simultaneously.

Cyberpunk set the record for most pre-orders ever almost exactly six years ago when eight million of you committed to the game before it had been released. A lot of you were left disappointed due to the fact that Cyberpunk then went on to have one of the most infamously disastrous launches in gaming history. It has redeemed itself multiple times over since then, and the odds of GTA 6 falling foul of the same fate are basically zero.

According to the latest data shared by Sensor Tower, GTA 6 has been pre-ordered 1.98 million times in the last week alone, clearly due to the hype for the game really starting to ramp up with less than two weeks to go until launch. That almost certainly means GTA 6 will rack up another two million pre-orders between now and release day, amassing a record that may never be broken.

Sensor Tower's data also reveals how many of you have pre-ordered on PS5 vs. Xbox Series X|S. The split has been a hotly debated topic, with stats claiming PS5 pre-orders were outselling their Xbox equivalent at a rate of eight-to-one. Turns out things aren't that bad for Xbox, although the split is far from even. 75% of GTA 6 pre-orders have been placed on PS5, so PlayStation has three times as many people prepping for what will likely be the biggest launch of all time compared to its Xbox rival.

You might be wondering who on Earth doesn't know about GTA 6 by this point, at least when it comes to people who might want to buy it ready for release day. You'd be surprised. While news about it has dominated the video game space for pretty much all of 2026, and it has broken containment to a degree, there are still people out there who will be playing on November 19 who either don't know GTA 6 is coming, or for whom it isn't front of mind so they haven't pre-ordered it yet. This last big marketing push, which includes an entire range of merch at high end brand selfridges, is for them, and will ensure GTA 6 continues to sell millions of copies before it has even been released.

#4220. Crimson Desert PC specs don't keep resolution and framerate targets a secret, and they don't use upscaling for everything either

Finally, a PC specification list that actually indicates resolution and framerate targets, and doesn't leave console players behind.

Crimson Desert is a little over one week away from release, and developer Pearl Abyss has delivered the official, final list of specs for the game. The twist is that the specs not only include useful information for PC players, they also cover similarly relevant details for console players, who traditionally don’t get mentioned in those reveals.

The specs are decently detailed, but more surprisingly - except for a single instance - they don’t include upscaling on PC, another thing games have gotten too comfortable using, even with their lowest specs.

On the official Crimson Desert website, developer Pearl Abyss has delivered a chunky post breaking down five different sets of PC requirements for the upcoming open-world action RPG. Each set indicates the graphics preset being used - and crucially, the resolution and framerate targets you can expect with each.

With the exception of the Minimum spec, all other presets do not appear to rely on upscaling of any kind. They do not say, however, whether ray tracing is being used with any of them, which is a feature that will throw all of those specs out of whack.

That same transparency also extends to non-PC platforms, which traditionally get few, if any, details about their own resolution and framerate targets. The console set of specs are extensive, just like PC, covering both PlayStation, and Xbox.

It’s granular enough to indicate which upscaling tech is being used, where applicable. This is relevant for owners of a PS5 Pro, a console that has access to Sony’s PSSR upscaling, alongside the standard AMD FSR tech the base console - and Xbox - use.

The developer has also revealed the base resolution for each mode across each console, and the resolution the image will be upscaled to using whichever tech is being utilised.

And, if you’re one of the five people who play games on Mac, you’ll be thrilled to know that the specs also include a section for Mac devices, split between the different Mac chips. The quality preset being used with each is not clear, however.

Finally, there's a set of specs for the Rog Xbox Ally, covering both the X and S models.

Crimson Desert arrives March 20 on PC, PS5, and Xbox Series X/S. You can expect more coverage from us at release and beyond.

#4219. Murals Preview: Frantic Fairy Tale Fun

Scott Baird is a Contributor from the UK with over a decade of video game writing experience.

Fairy tales have been deconstructed and shown through a modern lens so many times that subversions are almost as common as straight tellings of the original stories. Murals is an upcoming action RPG that takes a comedic, subversive look at classic kids' stories, wrapped in an addictive gameplay loop familiar to fans of the big hits of the past few years.

Roguelike action RPGs have exploded in popularity, especially on PC, with gamers becoming hooked on brutally difficult gameplay merged with random elements that offer near-infinite replayability. On the surface, Murals seems cut from the same cloth as something like Hades, being an action RPG with an isometric viewpoint, where a long hero dashes around, avoiding attacks, while unleashing an increasingly larger arsenal at their foes.

DualShockers visited developer Dlala Studios at their home base for a hands-on preview of Murals. This consisted of playing the first two chapters and experiencing an in-development build of the game that is still being tweaked and worked on. What’s here is impressive, especially in terms of the aesthetics, with gorgeous visuals on display for Murals’ fairy-tale world.

The Murals preview I played featured two stages: Little Briar Rose (the story that formed the basis for Sleeping Beauty), and Rapunzel. The story starts with the protagonist, whose appearance can best be described as “Player 2 April O’Neil,” waking up in a mysterious new world with no memory of how they got there.

The protagonist of Murals doesn't talk much, but when they do, they have branching dialogue options. Sadly, the game immediately says that these have no bearing on the gameplay and are just for flavor, so the choices may as well not exist. While I'm not expecting some Mass Effect-style consequences for every dialogue choice, it'd be nice if some of the responses had some kind of bearing on the gameplay.

The protagonist doesn't talk much because they're soon joined by Loaf, the game's mascot character. Loaf is a poorly drawn doodle that resembles an eraser with lizard-like plates on its back. Loaf quickly sets the comedic tone of the story, with Monty Python-esque retorts to the silliness of their situation, before the two are joined by Slash Gordon, the player’s trusty blade.

The chapters of Murals I experienced involved solving the locals' problems, such as helping an insomniac Sleeping Beauty or freeing a trapped Rapunzel by climbing her hair up the tower. There was also an overarching story involving a mysterious being known as The Creator, who looks like a smug art critic and seems to pull the strings from afar, guiding the protagonist along.

Twisted Tower is a terrifyingly twisted fairy tale that's done its homework.

One reliable ally the player has between battles is Magic Dave, voiced by legendary UK comedian Bob Mortimer. He’s the Resident Evil 4 Merchant of the game, providing upgrades (called Eeries) between stages, while exchanging witty banter with Toast.

The comedy in Murals is going to be love it or hate it. Saying it’s steeped in British irreverence is an understatement, and that sentence alone might be off-putting to some. A great comparison is the works of the late great Terry Pratchett: that provides a metric of Britishness the player should expect.

Dlala Studios is no stranger to pretty 2D games, having previously created the modern Battletoads game, as well as Disney Illusion Island. Murals marks the studio's departure from established intellectual properties and into publishing, which is why fairy tales were the company's next stop, since they're in the public domain.

Easily the high point of Murals is its visuals. Each level in Murals is a stunning, hand-drawn piece of artwork, where every room appears lovingly crafted and filled with little touches to admire while exploring.

Each level in Murals is a stunning, hand-drawn piece of artwork, with every room lovingly crafted and filled with little touches to admire while exploring. The same is true of the character artwork, with everything polished to perfection. The level of detail is especially impressive, considering Murals is still being developed, yet the team already has the aesthetic nailed down.

What once started out as a subgenre of NES classics has now become a typically hand-drawn set of video games that never fail to impress.

The only exception to the pretty visuals is the enemies in Murals, which are 3D models and nowhere near as visually impressive as the stages or NPCs. The monsters are quite generic and don't feel like they match the fairy-tale world they exist in, with designs that could fit into pretty much any action RPG.

The boss monsters are similarly whelming, with the giant frog faced in the Little Briar Rose stage doing the same jumping attack over and over again, only adding mobs to his move pool. In contrast, the final encounter of the Rapunzel stage is just waves of enemies, with no big boss in sight.

Fairy tales are full of creative villains who could be repurposed for use in video games. Just look at The Wolf Among Us for only one example among many. The enemies in Murals need an injection of creativity in both their design and battle strategy if the game wants to keep the player's interest.

It's impossible to play Murals and not compare it to Hades or its sequel. Just looking at a gameplay video on the Steam page, the comparisons are easy to see. It’s impossible to deny that Murals has Hades DNA, with the same basic combat loop, even though it takes a drastically different approach.

In Murals, the player has a choice of melee weapons (the sword named Slash Gordon and the hammer called the Wolfhammer in the demo), a ranged weapon with recharging ammo, and a super move that builds up over the battle, all of which are used to destroy foes. The player can dash to avoid enemy attacks and must survive waves of enemies through chains of rooms, with liberal health drops between areas.

As someone who was brutalized by Hades 2 in the past, one mechanic in Murals' combat immediately stuck out. When swinging a weapon or using a ranged attack, it's possible to perform a dash and gain invincibility frames. This makes the combat significantly easier than in similar games, as the player doesn't have to commit to attacks in the same way as they would in, say, a FromSoftware game, leaving them locked into a position where they can be countered.

Sébastien Benard's action roguelike has resurfaced with a release window after several years of radio silence.

The quick dash is more effective when using Slash Gordon, as it synergizes well with a swift weapon. This isn't to say that the Wolfhammer isn't also broken in its own way, as it has a breath weapon-style attack that can be merged with a Frost Rune to perform multiple hits that each have a chance of inflicting the Freeze status effect on an enemy, drastically increasing the chance of paralyzing them.

This makes the combat significantly easier than in similar games, as the player doesn't have to commit to attacks in the same way as they would in, say, a FromSoftware game, leaving them locked into a position where they can be countered.

Murals is still a work-in-progress, so there’s plenty of time for developers to tweak the gameplay balance. What’s here is considerably easier than many of the action RPGs on the market, but the reason for that could be related to the fact that it’s a mostly linear, story-based game, with few roguelike elements.

The levels in Murals might look like the randomly connected rooms of countless roguelikes, but the stages have been crafted and designed to tell a story, including NPC encounters, puzzles, and even side quests. While there are some random elements, such as how the upgrades/Eeries are handled, the bulk of the game is a planned affair, which explains why it’s easier than its contemporaries.

Each level in Murals is a stunning, hand-drawn piece of artwork, where every room appears lovingly crafted and filled with little touches to admire while exploring

It's a bold move to go for a linear approach in a market so consumed with randomness, especially when Murals uses a gameplay style and overall aesthetic that’s tied to roguelikes. That being said, there’s plenty of room for a more focused and narrative-driven title that uses the gameplay loop of familiar titles, especially when the levels look this good.

Murals has a ton of potential and an amazing pedigree behind it. Dlala Studios has produced some amazing titles in the past, and the fact that the game is so polished and impressive at this point in development is a feat unto itself. The hard part is going to be tweaking the combat to make it satisfying for everyone, meaning some strict difficulty modifiers could be the answer.

The comedic writing and tone in Murals are trickier, as they're so baked into the game’s identity, yet also have the potential to miss the mark. It’s the kind of thing that someone will know they’re going to enjoy within a short period of time, and hopefully, Mural’s subversive take on fairy tales is as appealing to the audience as its combat.

#4218. Battlefield 6 is getting a free trial next week with a decent selection of maps and modes

Battlefield 6's second-ever free trial, and the first in 2026, is upon us.

Battlefield Studios has announced that Battlefield 6 is going free to play for one week next week. Well, a portion of the game is, anyway, as part of a free trial that will include some of the game’s most popular modes and maps.

Though it does not encompass the entirety of the game, the free trial is fairly generous. Here’s what to expect.

For starters, the trial kicks off Tuesday, March 17 and will run until the following Tuesday, March 24. The trial will be accessible from Battlefield Redsec, the already free-to-play portion of the game.

Once downloaded, you’ll find a new Battlefield 6 Free Trial section in the main menu. Because Redsec and Battlefield 6 multiplayer share progression, if you played the former at any point, you’ll be able to pick up from where you left off.

The same is also true the other way around; if this is your first time with Battlefield 6, all your unlocks will carry over to the full version, as well as to Redsec if you decide stick with the free-to-play off-shoot.

Once it kicks off, you’ll find three playlists to choose from. Casual Breakthrough, All-out Warfare, and a third playlist showcasing the new Nightfall game mode and its associated map.

All-out Warfare is what you come to Battlefield for, and that playlist features Conquest, Breakthrough, as well as BF6’s newcomer Escalation - all large-scale, combined arms game modes. They will be playable across four maps. You get to play on two from Season 2: Contaminated, and Hagental Base, one from Season 1: Eastwood, and Mirak Valley from the base game.

Casual Breakthrough is based on a playlist that already exists in the core game, and it’s really designed as a nice on-ramp for new players. It also offers less intense gameplay, perfect for people grinding unlocks.

Casual Breakthrough is limited to just 16 real players (eight per team), with the rest filled up with bots. You earn the same amount of XP in those matches, except when you interact with bots, so killing a bot will net less than a human player. Outside of that, unlocks, Challenges and all other things that don’t depend on stat-tracking can be done within.

In the trial, the Casual Breakthrough playlist includes Hagental Base, Contaminated, and Eastwood.

The most interesting is the third playlist, in part because its content will also be available to owners of the full game for the first time right alongside free-to-play players. Nightfall is a playlist exclusive to the Hagental Base map.

This is a very small map, so the mode selection here is Team Deathmatch, Squad Deathmatch, and Domination. Under Nightfall conditions, lights across the entire map are turned off, so you’re going to have use your NVGs to be able to see. This is also a god opportunity to try out weapon attachments that specifically work under low-light conditions, which typically don’t get much use in multiplayer.

March 17 also marks the launch of the second stage of Battlefield 6’s Season 2, which comes with the aforementioned Nightfall content, as well as a big new update - so the timing works out nicely for everyone.

#4217. Dandori Academy Is The Perfect Addition To Pikmin 4 Switch 2 Edition For Major Pikmin Fans

Pikmin 4's Switch 2 Edition brings some welcome upgrades to the original game, but whether they're worth the cost depends on your love for Pikmin.

While Mario might be the face of Nintendo, there’s no doubt that Pikmin also holds a special place in Shigeru Miyamoto's heart, as evidenced by the recent Pikmin Day Nintendo Direct. Although there is still no word that we’ll be getting Pikmin 5 anytime soon, Pikmin 4 is thankfully getting some new features to help tide players over as part of the Pikmin 4 Nintendo Switch 2 Edition plus Dandori Academy.

Whether you’ve already played the original and are considering the $10 upgrade pack, or never picked it up and are thinking about grabbing the full Switch 2 Edition now, it’s important to know what to expect. Switch 2 Editions aren’t a new idea, as several games have already received the same treatment, but no two have been exactly alike.

Tears of the Kingdom’s Switch 2 Edition reduced load times and introduced compatibility with the Zelda Notes app. Meanwhile, games like Mario Party Jamboree received an entirely new game mode that utilized the Switch 2’s exclusive features. Pikmin 4’s Switch 2 Edition falls somewhere between those two.

Pikmin 4 was already a decent-looking game when it released on the original Switch, so it should come as no surprise that even though it displays in 4K when docked, there’s no truly noticeable difference in visuals between the Switch 2 Edition and just playing the original version on your Switch 2. At least not one significant enough to note.

That said, even though the visuals didn’t need an upgrade, there are a few welcome changes to the gameplay. Alongside the addition of GameShare support for Dandori Battles, the biggest change comes in the primary game mode, more specifically, to Pikmin 4’s adorable alien pup, Oatchi.

Rather than relying solely on your button inputs to command Oatchi, you can now say the command directly into the mic. I did have to mess with the feature’s settings a little before I could use it properly, though.

Default settings don’t filter out background noise, so the sounds of my TV and toddler were causing Oatchi to rush around wildly without a direct command. Then, filtering out too much sound forced me to yell directly into the mic for the command to work. However, once I found the sweet spot for my environment, it became a surprisingly useful feature.

For one thing, Oatchi didn't appear to take time to charge up his Rush when obeying voice commands, so it’s quicker and more convenient, which is great when targeting moving enemies. I ended up using it more than I anticipated, and appreciated that it was optional so I could turn it off when I didn’t want to disturb anyone. It might be a small change, but it’s a fun and welcome one.

Given the minor changes to Pikmin 4’s base game, the addition of Dandori Academy is the main reason to pick up its Switch 2 Edition. Dandori Academy is an additional game mode that can be accessed from the game’s title screen and played without progressing the primary story mode at all. It consists of timed mini-games that test your skills at collecting treasure and delegating tasks to your Pikmin.

You’re free to do practice mini-games as often as you’d like, but every Friday, Saturday, and Sunday there will be an Exam Event. The exams are a way to show how well all your Dandori practice has paid off, especially since you only get one attempt per exam, and you’ll be awarded a medal based on your score. Certain scores can even earn you points towards rewards, including for the Pikmin Bloom mobile app.

You do need an active Nintendo Switch Online membership to share high scores online and access specific rewards, so keep that in mind if you plan to participate in exams.

There are three difficulty levels for the exam – Elementary, Advanced, and Graduate – with two exams per difficulty.

Overall, the Dandori Academy mini-games aren’t that different from everything you do in the main game. That said, the time limit does add some intensity, and I appreciate that there’s no single right way to earn a high score, so you do have to challenge yourself to use different strategies. For example, some players might prioritize collecting treasure at the start, while others focus on increasing their Pikmin count first.

I also found that even Elementary difficulty proved a bit of a challenge, so if you’re worried that things will be too easy, I don’t think that should be a major concern. If you’re like me and find collecting treasure one of the most fun parts of Pikmin, it’s easy to spend hours in practice mode, which also benefits you beyond just improving your skill.

Completing multiple practice sessions earns you Redo Passes, which will allow you to retake an exam if you don't get the score you want. There is a cap on these, so you can’t farm them indefinitely, but it is nice that your hard work earns you a second chance on an exam you might’ve accidentally botched.

Overall, Pikmin 4 Switch 2 Edition improves on everything that was already great about Pikmin 4. It’s still a charming game that offers more hours of fun gameplay than some of Nintendo’s other titles, now with a few extra features to improve the game’s quality of life.

As for whether it’s worth the upgrade or extra cost, I think that comes down to how interested you are in Dandori Academy. Since the exams themselves require you to hop into the game every weekend, and you need Nintendo Switch Online to enjoy the full benefits, I worry that most players might not be all that interested.

All the mini-games are incredibly fun, don’t get me wrong. I just can’t realistically see myself or many others logging in every weekend to participate in exams beyond the first month or two, so I can only recommend this to those who genuinely love Pikmin, utilize the Pikmin Bloom app, or have been looking for a way to ease the wait for the unannounced, but increasingly likely, Pikmin 5.

#4216. Petit Planet Hands-On Preview – Creature Comforts

Petit Planet marks Hoyoverse’s maiden voyage into the life sim genre popularized by games like Animal Crossing, Stardew Valley, and, most recently, Pokémon Pokopia. The creators of Genshin Impact, Honkai: Star Rail, and Zenless Zone Zero have crafted well-received, lucrative free-to-play gacha games across several disparate genres; Petit Planet, fittingly, sees it try to attract yet another world of players. It’s been a year since I first played Petit Planet’s initial alpha test, and I spent a couple of more hours exploring its cozy cosmos at the Hoyoverse Media Tour in Seoul, South Korea. Although what I played has not dramatically changed my opinion of the game – it remains a delightful, if familiar, good time – speaking to its lead designer who goes by the single name Murphy and lead artist Yunli Huang helped shed light on how Petit Planet will differentiate itself from contemporaries and its approach to multiplayer, storytelling, and monetization.

The game’s premise centers on a customizable protagonist who sets out to populate their own personal planet (which is about the size of King Kai’s world from Dragon Ball Z). Although you are ostensibly human, everyone else is a talking animal. Your mentor of sorts is a chillax sheepdog named Mobai, who enjoys wearing straw hats and dropping his catchphrase/life mantra “Mo worries” and “Mo Rush.” The business-minded Glenn the Squirrel is a shopkeeper and seems like a cuter, less aggressive Tom Nook. Yunghou is a shy fox who enjoys farming and has the slightest hint of a southern accent. These critters and many more inhabit your planet, which you’ll grow from an empty (but vibrant) rock into a bustling village filled with homes, businesses, crops, decor, and, of course, neighbors.

Story is rarely a hook for a genre that largely promotes creating your own fun through the emergent moments with your neighbors and friends in multiplayer. Still, after Pokémon Pokopia presented an unexpectedly wild and fascinating tale, I ask if players should bother getting invested in a grander narrative à la Genshin Impact. The short answer seems to be “not so much.”

“Unlike other Hoyoverse games, there is no such main plot,” Murphy explains in my group interview. “There will be a main story at the beginning, but the main purpose is just to guide the players, get more familiar with the setting and the world. But the whole narrative of this game will be more fragmented. For example, if you look at those descriptions of those items, there will be a lot of content and narrative behind it. If you look at the description of creatures, many of them are real creatures in real world, and you get to learn more knowledge of this creature by reading those descriptions. And also, we've developed a very comprehensive narrative for each of our neighbors, so that is also part of our, called like, main plot, main narrative, because we want to make this world more like more lively and a more livable world. So that is how we treat narrative in this game."

While players who enjoy a substantial story to propel them through a game may be disappointed, those looking to unwind with a laid-back experience should be pleased. Hoyoverse is designing Petit Planet to be a no-pressure experience to enjoy at your leisure, hence why it emphasizes it as a life sim more than a management sim. There are no complicated stats to manage; simple inputs make it easy to pick up and play; imperfection is encouraged, with Hoyoverse comparing the experience to doodling as a child: your creation may not be perfect, but you had fun bringing your imagination to life.

I spent the first hour of my roughly two-and-a-half-hour session starting from scratch to see if any notable changes were made to this introductory portion in the last year. If there are any differences, they’re imperceptible because I wen went through the same onboarding of learning how to catch bugs and fish, building your first home, inviting your first neighbor, and farming crops, all while growing a magical sapling that, after performing enough tasks, blooms into a full tree that brings new life and mechanics to your world as it grows. Performing special tasks for residents, from completing requests to simply interacting with them, grows their bond, which, when high enough, will entice them to move in. For veteran genre fans, it’s a familiar song and dance. What I did notice this time around is how refreshingly quick the onboarding is. You have all of these foundational mechanics within the first 45 to 50 minutes, which is a nice pace. It was a good refresher for some foundational mechanics I’d forgotten since I last played, but it created an appetite to dive deeper.

Thankfully, Hoyoverse provided a second build set many hours into the game to give an idea of how planets can evolve. This build was set during winter, one of Petit Planet’s revolving seasons that alter the environment and introduce themed cosmetics and decor for players and residents. Sporting winter gear, I ran around the snow-covered planet, which was densely populated with shops, homes, and neighbors. I was initially greeted by unfamiliar faces named Trixie and Kookoo, who provided weather forecasts and news reports reminiscent of Isabelle from Animal Crossing and Callie and Marie from Splatoon. My sparse quest log was tricky to tackle since they revolved around mechanics I had no context for, such as setting up Vignettes. These are essentially templates for unique scenes filled out by dropping the correct furniture pieces in their layout; in this case, I had to set up an outdoor movie on the beach.

I only spent roughly an hour with this late build, and my biggest takeaway was simply how dense and lovely the village looked. A lot of work went into crafting this build, which boasted a farm filled with different crops (with unlockable recipes to create dishes from them), crafting tables to build furniture from collectible blueprints, and several shops, including Glenn’s to purchase a revolving selection of decor items. None of what I saw surprised me, however. Petit Planet so far checks many of the boxes you’d expect and want from a life sim. My cursory tour of a later-game planet did little to reveal any big new ideas, but what I did experience seemed perfectly cromulent.

My biggest question regards multiplayer. As much as I enjoy Animal Crossing: New Horizons and Pokémon Pokopia as solo experiences, playing with friends feels like a mean joke because of the tedious number of hoops to jump through just to invite other players into your world. And even once your buddy arrives, interactions are disappointingly limited. When I ask if Petit Planet offers a comparatively frictionless multiplayer experience, Murphy vaguely assures smoother sailing. “The multiplayer experience is a very important part of our game because, just as the interaction with NPCs, the interaction with other players is also a form of building up emotional connection to this game, and we want to provide that kind of experience to our players.” More specifically, Murphy cites features such as dynamic server load adjustments based on player counts and the option to allow or ban visiting players from taking resources from your planet to prevent griefing.

As a free-to-play Hoyoverse game, monetization is a major talking point. In Petit Planet’s case, the team agrees that rolling for neighbors gacha-style would be strange and defeats the spirit of the genre. Instead, all monetization will revolve around cosmetics; players can unlock new furniture and themed decor sets, outfits, and other cosmetic accessories for their character. Unlocking a full themed set of decor earns currency points, and there are myriad reward meters to fill for performing mundane tasks like greeting residents or catching bugs. It remains to be seen if and how Petit Planet’s progression begins nudging players into opening their wallets, but Hoyoverse promises it will be an experience that deemphasizes grinding.

I also briefly checked out the recently announced Switch 2 version of Petit Planet. My impressions after about 15 minutes of playtime: it’s fine. It sometimes ran noticeably hitchier than the PC version I spent most of my time with, but it seems perfectly adequate so far and, hopefully, will be a smooth experience when it launches sometime next year.

Since life sims require more than a couple of hours to fully reveal their quality, it was tough to get a read on Petit Planet even with this new showing. The game looks beautiful thanks to Hoyoverse’s signature sharp and colorful visual style. It has a relaxing vibe, and feels mechanically decent for the most part. In short, it seems broadly fine and like a respectable take on the genre. I suspect its biggest appeal will be that it will receive what Animal Crossing: New Horizons lacked: years of constant, substantial support.

Hoyoverse is very good about keeping fans of its games well fed with regular updates for years on end, and I don’t expect it to stop now. The idea of a seemingly well-made spin on Animal Crossing that’s free to download and, unless it completely bombs, will almost certainly receive years of new content is enticing on paper. I imagine this is the reason Petit Planet is coming to Switch 2 next year, where it can lure in Animal Crossing and Pokopia players before other consoles. PC and mobile players, meanwhile, must only wait until December 4 when Petit Planet fully launches to see if it has the chops to stand alongside the coziest giants of the genre.

#4215. Honkai: Star Rail Version 4.1 livestream reveals a pared-back, four-week update as HoYo plays catch-up

Honkai: Star Rail will continue the Planarcadia story arc in Version 4.1, as the Star Rail Fest presents a new twist.

A new Honkai: Star Rail Special Program has concluded, which means some fresh news about the game’s upcoming major update. Version 4.1, unveiled today as Unraveled for Daybreak, is the action RPG’s next moment, kicking off on March 25.

Unraveled for Daybreak is the next chapter in the ongoing story of Planarcadia, with the Astra Express Crew now invited to a fan fest inspired by their own past journeys. The aptly named Star Rail Fest is ostensibly hosted to allow more of the citizens of Arcadia to experience the Trailblaze.

As everyone’s eyes is fixated on the grand Star Rail Fest, the Phantasmoon Games continue to be in full swing, as does the war with the Supplicants. Star Rail Fest is, however, the big focus of this update, in case it wasn't obvious.

The event is made up of three large-scale zones, each themed around past excursions of the Astral Express. You’ll get to explore the Belobog Zone, Xianzhou Luofu Zone, and Penacony Zone. Later on, you’ll also be able to visit Pearluxe Tower, the headquarters of Pearluxe Corp.

Each area will feature its own attractions, such as the balloon figures of Supreme Guardian Cocolia and the Destruction Engine, the duel against the Lord Ravager Phantylia at Scalegorge Waterscape, and the Pearluxe Tower’s Alloy King Pom-Pom model.

The hot new arrival is bumbling noirish detective Ashveil whom we've met in Version 4.0, and who becomes a playable character with this update. Ashveil is a 5-Star Lightning-Type character, on the Path of The Hunt. You’ll be able to pull for him throughout 4.1's runtime, which is slightly reduced at four weeks instead of the usual six, in order to rebalance the schedule after the extra-long Version 3.8.

In combat, Ashveil is capable of increasing Crit Damage of all allies. He can also mark an enemy as Bait, which reduces the Defence of all enemies on the field so long as this tag holds. If Ashveil uses his Skill on the baited target, he will deal extra Damage and regain Skill Points for the team.

Ashveil can bully that baited target even further by launching Hounding Pursuit. If any of his teammates attacks the Bait, he can further deliver a follow-up attack that gradually accumulates Gluttony for as long as he’s in combat. Gluttony can later be consumed to boost follow-up attack damage.

If he lands a kill, Ashveil continues to deal damage to the next enemy he attacks. That buff is transferred if that enemy is killed. Even in map exploration, Ashveil can be deadly, capable of inflicting Stunned upon enemies within a specific range.

Returning characters this patch will be Hyacine in the first half, and Boothill in the second half. Once again, due to the reduced runtime, their banner reruns will be slightly shorter than normal, at just two weeks each instead of three — so be sure to take that into account if you're planning on pulling for either of them.

Version 4.1 also adds the Wispae War Saga, a new activity where you can practice your leadership skills by commanding different types of Wispae Soldiers in the Graphia Academy. You can upgrade each one, use spell cards to alter their effects, and later face other champions. You ultimately want to play this to unlock new Wispae Companions, not to mention complete the challenges within.

Finally, Version 4.1 marks the start of a new Arcadian Chronicles phase in the Divergent Universe. You’ll be able to use Waypoint Pass cards to explore the different areas. HoYo is also bringing back Planar Fissure and Garden of Plenty with double rewards. And as ever, if you log in for at least seven days after downloading the new patch, you’ll earn 10 premium banner pulls.

#4214. UK Charts: Zelda: Ocarina Of Time Is The Second Biggest UK Launch In Franchise History

The latest charts data from the UK is in, and as expected, The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time has debuted at the top spot, beating out the likes of Modern Warfare 4 and FC 27.

While not surprising, it's nevertheless a satisfying result, and we'd be keen to see what the actual split is between physical copies and digital. We suspect that, with the pre-order bonuses and midnight launches, physical has likely vastly outsold digital in this case.

In fact, Chris Dring from The Game Business has stated that Ocarina of Time is the second biggest UK physical launch in franchise history, beating Breath of the Wild by around 35% but falling short of Tears of the Kingdom by about half. However, he states that there are "plenty of install base-related reasons for both of those things". He also states that this is easily the biggest physical launch of 2026 so far.

Elsewhere, Godzilla: Destroy All Monsters Melee Remastered has made its debut at number 9, with Switch 2 putting up a solid fight against the PS5. Stellar Blade Complete Edition has also done rather well to land at number 12; a solid indication that there is decent demand for proper physical games on Switch 2.

Here's the full top 40, with platform breakdowns for games available on Switch, Switch 2, and other consoles:

#4213. Zenless Zone Zero Version 2.7 brings Angels of Delusion to the battlefield with playable Nangong Yu

Champions Never Fall to the Past indeed, as Zenless Zone Zero prepares for a major update that fans of Angels of Delusion will appreciate.

HoYoverse has delivered another Special Program for the second day running, this time for Zenless Zone Zero. The developer revealed the full details of Version 2.7, subtitled Champions Never Fall to the Past.

This next major update arrives March 24, adding two new Agents, and introducing the Hollow Champion competition.

Most things in Version 2.7 follow on from the Hollow Champion competition, which brings together old friends and familiar faces, as well interesting newcomers. Everyone is in it to win some big rewards and earn glory.

Among the unexpected participants the competition has attracted are the Public Security's Metropolitan Order Division, and even some former Calydon's Sweepers. A big challenge that awaits is Black Wolf Romeul, who’s capable of increasing his Crit Damage Resistance and Interruption Resistance by activating a Corruptive Barrier.

Romeul can also cause enemies to continuously lose HP, but you can beat him by putting together a squad that can deal sustained Anomaly damage, which will break through the barrier quickly.

Our first new arrival in Version 2.7 is Cissia of the Metropolitan Order Division. She is an S-Rank Electric Attack Agent who automatically gains three stacks of Venom when she enters the battle. Each stack deals Electric Damage while also increasing her Crit Rate for a time.

When she runs out of Venom, which will happen, Cissia can generate more stacks by using her EX Special Attack. She can also use her Basic Attack, Serpent's Kiss, to better utilise the new stacks of Venom she generates.

The other new Agent may be the more exciting. Nangong Yu, the captain and lead dancer of the Angels of Delusion, can now be part of your team. Nangong Yu is an S-Rank Ether Stun Agent who can boost her team’s Anomaly Buildup Rate against Stunned enemies.

Being part of an idol group has its perks, because she automatically regenerates Downbeat as time goes on, and even more any time a squad member inflicts an enemy with Anomaly. Nangong Yu can then use Downbeat - after enough has been accumulated - on charged attacks that keep enemies stunned for longer. Her Ultimate triggers Ether Veil: Delusion Reprise, which boosts the entire squad’s Attack.

Returning Agents in Version 2.7 will be Yidhari, the S-Rank Ice Rupture Agent, as well as Seed, the Electric Attack Agent.

Outside of all the very important action in the core story, this chapter also brings new themed events to Lumina Square’s Simmer Hot Pot Restaurant. The Simulated Battle Trial is also getting some love, with updated mechanics and new enemy line-ups.

Catch up on our recently updated Zenless Zone Zero character tier list, and don’t forget to check out these Zenless Zone Zero codes before you jump in for some free stuff.

#4212. Heartopia goes to the movies with its next event

Heartopia's Whale Island will soon host a new event that's all about the magic of cinema.

Heartopia’s next in-game event has been announced, and it’s one you may not have seen coming. Developer XD Games revealed Dreamlight Cinematics Festival, an upcoming limited-time event that celebrates cinema and movie-making.

Dreamlight Cinematics kicks off March 21, and will run through May 1, available across the game’s PC and mobile versions.

Dreamlight Cinematics Festival takes place on Whale Island. And, perhaps as an unofficial Oscars tie-in, it’s all about classic Hollywood filmmaking. Not only that, it also celebrates the aesthetics and industrial design of that era.

All around the game’s world, you’ll be able to find festival-themed collectables, which you can then use to unlock free Time-Limited Exhibition Passes.

If you log in during the event’s runtime, you’ll get the Car Cinema furniture set for free. This cosmetic bundle comes with chairs that are modelled after vintage vehicles, as well as poster display stands with unique movie making-themed decorations.

If you’re looking to spend some money, the Deluxe Festival Pack comes with a large Island Sunset Billboard, which you can place outside your home so everyone knows you spent that money. The same pack also comes with the Popcorn Movie Ticket chat bubble skin, and a 10% bonus to Festival Tokens when you sell stuff at the store.

Regardless of which pack you get, you’ll earn collection points for each, which puts you on the path to unlocking outfits like the Dreamlight Cinematics Festival-specific Modern Show Dandy and Modern Show Belle. There’s also a Cinematic Moments building material set launching with this event.

For now, we have the above reveal trailer to go on, which does offer some idea of what it’s going to look like in-game. Until things kick off on the weekend, you best arm yourself with some Heartopia codes.

Nintendo and LEGO have teased the next entry in their 'Adults Welcome' Mario range, which will see Yoshi step into the limelight.

While we haven't seen the full set just yet, a new post on the Nintendo Today! app shows everything we need to know. We can see a close-up of the dino's eyes and snout in brick form, accompanied by the message, "Hatching soon".

Whether the set ends up being anything more than just Yoshi remains to be seen (we got that Super Mario World-inspired one a few years back, with a pixel art Mario in tow, let's not forget), but more Mario big builds are always a good thing.

The other sworded issue will be the price. The previous '18+' builds have come with a rather hefty price tag (the Mario and Luigi Kart sets will set you back £149.99 / £159.99 respectively), so we'd be surprised if the upcoming Yoshi isn't more of the same.

We'll be keeping an eye out for more price details and the all-important release date over the coming weeks.

#4210. Xbox Series X-BITE Alligator Console Returns With A New Video And Multiple New Images

The original trailer has already done over 1 million views

Earlier this week, Xbox unveiled a new custom console that we described as their most "insane" yet, and within just a few days, it's already racked up over 1 million views on the official Xbox YouTube channel.

There's a lot of hype around this thing, then, which explains why Xbox has teamed up with Complex and rapper Lil' Baby to reveal a new video and lots more images of the Xbox Series X-BITE in action.

For those who haven't been keeping up, the Xbox Series X-BITE is a functional console that sits inside of an alligator, and it appears to be inspired by GTA 6 (but for marketing reasons, Xbox can't say that!).

Here's a look at the new video, and we'll throw the new images below it:

There's apparently only one of these in the world, and it's been designed by John Nolan Studio - an animatronics specialist that has worked on some major Hollywood productions including Jurassic Park in the past.

The only way to win the Xbox alligator console is by entering the official sweepstakes, which is taking place across various social media platforms as we speak. Entries end on November 10th, so you haven't got long to enter.

We really hope the eventual winner ends up enjoying the system for themselves instead of flogging it for an insane amount of money, but we can't exactly blame them if they end up picking the latter option!

In any case, this is an extremely cool custom console, and maybe even the most elaborate in Xbox history.

#4209. All the hype has already made Crimson Desert one of the biggest launches on Steam this year

We're merely days away from the end of the first quarter of 2026, and Crimson Desert has come in clutch to join the list of big sellers.

Crimson Desert, the open-world action RPG off-shoot from Korean MMO Black Desert Online, has officially launched, nearly six years after it was initially revealed. The game has been building up a lot of momentum over the years, which recently coalesced to turn it into one of 2026’s most anticipated titles.

All of it has been leading up to this moment, and the game appears to have landed smoothly, though not without controversy, as has seemingly become part of its MO.

It has not been 24 hours since Crimson Desert launched on PC and consoles, and it’s already become a big hit. On Steam, one of two stores where the game can be purchased (the other being the Epic Games Store), the game shot to the top of the charts.

The action RPG continued to accumulate more and more players on Steam, peaking at a very respectable 239,045 concurrent players (via SteamDB). Though its success was very much expected, we perhaps didn’t predict its peak would be that high.

Indeed, Crimson Desert has been in Steam’s top 100 global sellers list for six weeks, jumping up six spots to become the number one seller this week just before it launched. As we get closer to the weekend, the numbers could climb even higher.

This peak concurrent puts Crimson Desert in the same league as several of the other major releases of the first quarter of 2026. The top spot continues to belong to Slay the Spire 2, which peaked at a staggering 574,638 concurrent players. It happened just days after the juggernaut Resident Evil Requiem achieved its own 344,214 peak concurrent, which was the year’s highest up until Slay the Spire 2’s release. All three are well ahead of Nioh 3’s 88,045 peak concurrent, and Marathon’s nearly identical peak of 88,337.

Crimson Desert has seen something of a mixed reception by critics. James gave it three stars in our review, saying it “lacks the connective sinew to be truly functional,” which is a common criticism shared by other outlets. Many also lamented the sheer number of systems fighting for player attention, its poorly explained mechanics, and counterintuitive controls.

On Steam, at least, players have similarly been divided, with the current Steam user rating sitting at Mixed, based on 8,728 reviews. Unsurprisingly, most of the negative reactions fall on the clunky controls and the game’s tendency to, as one Steam user put it, “so miserably tries to be everything at once, and fails to be anything at all.”

If you’re just getting started in Crimson Desert yourself, or plan to do so soon, we recommend reading these crucial tips to help orient yourself in the game’s vast world. You should also plan your initial skill unlocks by prioritising these skills to spend your Abyss Artifacts first.

#4208. Cyberpunk trading sim Probably Stolen is about running a kiosk in a space station full of gangs, megacorps, and secret rogue cyborgs

I will have you know this is an original Malorian Arms 3516

I have so far not been shivved, shanked, brain fried, hazed, wasted, ironed, short-circed, flat-lined or even complained at in Probably Stolen - Cyberpunk Shopkeeper Sim, but I'm sure it's just a matter of time.

In this neuromantic kiosk game from Questing Goose Studio, you're a new store owner aboard a backwater space station. Each day, you roll up the shutter and do business with a procession of shady types, ranging from janitors with unappetising beards to sexy cowled folk with Main Character tattoos. The basics are simple enough, for all the overwhelmingly menu-led presentation: buy what you can afford, according to your instinct for the wider market, sell what you can fit into the customer's budget. But things quickly get complicated.

You've got to watch out for wanted criminals, checking them against mugshots and possibly, reporting them to security. You've got to think about how your transactions shape the opinions of various factions, from revolutionaries through corpo bosses to the mob. You've got to run a magnifying glass over robot hands and cigarette packets, identifying vintage pieces and counterfeits. You've got to head out at night to scrounge stock from the dumps, preferably without getting shivved, shanked, etcetera. You've got to pay the electricity bill. You've got to shoot rogue androids in the CPU.

I've only peeked timidly over the counter of Probably Stolen, which I would cautiously characterise as Papers, Please with a lot more wheeling and dealing, but it feels like there's some decent substance here. I'm particularly intrigued by the idea of diversifying my operations beyond bog-standard checkout work.

"Start as a gunsmith, chemist, water merchant, fence, farmer, or from absolute rock bottom," the Steam page growls. "Every product line has its own profit curve and its own way of ruining you, weapons bring inspections, chemicals bring addiction, water brings liability, contraband brings raids. Some trades need heavy machinery and permits, others just a good hiding spot and a straight face. The better the margins, the worse the consequences when something goes wrong. You’re not choosing a theme for your shop, you’re choosing which kind of trouble you’re willing to monetize."

Oof! I'll use that closing line next time I interview a producer about season passes. Maybe I'll use it next time I have to pick a wallpaper pattern for my flat.

As cyberpunk fictions go, this does seem very comfortable. Your store has a cassette player with a selection of synthy music - I turned it off after 30 seconds, because the tunes were so gratingly generic. Dare I say it, cyberpunk is a "cosy" genre these days, but perhaps I just need to trade up to some classier earworms.

I also don't think much of Probably Stolen's writing, which seems clipped and flavourless, but it's getting the job done, and besides, I'm very early on in my career as a skanky pawnshop operator. I haven't even sold any toilet roll yet, and that feels like the real rite of passage. People who prefer their Netrunner 7-Elevens all 3D and hung with beautiful, beautiful birdcages might prefer the dives you get in No Law, which Julian saw recently.

#4207. Crimson Desert's first patch aims at fixing controls, but it mostly affects mouse and keyboard

The first post-launch patch for Crimson Desert is here, and the list of changes is promising, even if it doesn't go far enough to address some deeper issues.

Crimson Desert has been out for a few days now, and as positive as its been received by many players, the game suffers from several fundamental issues that anyone who’s played it has called out.

Perhaps the loudest one of those has been how the game controls, which is a problem that stems from the complexity of controls themselves, as well as the underlying animations behind many of the actions the player character performs.

In the first case, at least, something is being done.

Developer Pearl Abyss rolled out patch 1.00.03 for Crimson Desert on Monday. The patch is available now on Steam and PlayStation, with Xbox and the Epic Games Store following “at a later time.”

Today’s update follows a letter to players the developer issued on Saturday. The letter generally acknowledged player feedback, but specifically pointed to complaints about the game’s clunky controls as something of a focus for the team.

The action RPG has actually broken its launch peak concurrent player numbers over the weekend, though only by a few thousands more. Its Steam user review rating has also improved over the same period.

This latest update only includes an initial set of fixes, but Pearl Abyss vowed to keep working on addressing all other points of feedback. A highlight in 1.00.03 is the addition of a Storage at Howling Hill Camp, which can be used to store inventory items.

The most important changes, of course, affect how the game controls on keyboard and mouse. Pearl Abyss included several fixes and altered some of the default presets to make the experience less painful when playing the game with a keyboard and mouse.

There are sadly no changes to controllers, but it is something that the developer said we can expect to see in future patches. More improvements for keyboard and mouse setups are in the works, too.

Beyond the control changes, patch 1.00.03 also includes a set of gameplay tweaks, especially when it comes to enemy health and difficulty. It also makes fast travelling more convenient, and brings a few fixes to NPC dialogue. You can read the full change log on Steam.

If you’re deep in Crimson Desert already, we definitely recommend giving our guides a look. We recently added new pages to help you figure out where to socket your Abyss Gear, how to find Contribution Points - and where to spend them, as well as more generally helpful information like how to expand your inventory, and how to reveal the map.

#4206. GTA 6 has a smell reaction system, which immediately joins Red Dead Redemption 2's dynamically shrinking horse balls on Rockstar's list of immersive symbols of excess

Florida of course being full of smelly smells that smell...smelly

Any reminder of Red Dead Redemption 2's temperature sensitive horse testicles brings a smile to my face. In truth, I can't say I've ever zoomed in close enough to properly take in the spectacle of Arthur Morgan's mount having its nuts dynamically expand and contract based on whether he's riding through snowy mountains or across baking plains, but I do always get a kick out of knowing such a thing's happening as I play. To this point, the horse balls have been the most infamous or meme-worthy example of Rockstar's obsession with going all-in on realistic detail to an arguably unnecessary degree, one that borders on overindulgence which players could conceivably never notice if they weren't expressly told about it.

That philosophy's gone nowhere, so GTA 6 was always going to have a feature that'd become as much of a metaphor for excess as those beloved balls. It may well be the smell reaction system revealed in Edge's long read on the game.

According to this latest rundown of things in GTA 6 and how they were made, Rockstar devs at one point had to make a character react to a not nice smell for a specific bit of "explorable content" stuffed into the game. Cool. One person scrunching their face up to show things are getting stinky in one minigame or mission. Leave it at that.

They reportedly did not leave it at that, later going back to flesh out this one smell reaction into a broader system which other locations to inspire various degrees of face-scrunching by protagonists Lucia and Jason. Cue, in the demo of the game in action which Rockstar gave Edge, Jason walking into a house and starting to act like someone who's just walked into a shower-averse teenager's bedroom during a heatwave despite that not having been set up as part of a deliberately crafted encounter. It's horse ball-esque dynamic systems playing off each other, and voila, a man going eewwwwwwwwwwwww.

Would GTA 6 be any worse off if, as in previous entries, you weren't being shown as expressly which places the crim whose boots you're sharing finds a bit too pongy for their liking? Almost certainly not, but hey, when you've decided your business is taking the detail to levels other games could only dream of having the budget for, getting to the point where you're adding a fiftieth layer of icing to a cake so packed to the gills with different tastes and flourishes that your guests will struggle to appreciate or even notice them all unless you painstakingly point out each one is sort of inevitable.

Another layer of gold wrap on the Bugatti, another brick made of diamonds in a wall projected to be the most lucrative of all time, another farty stench in a room already drowning in foul aromas. It's beautiful in the perverse sort of way that I imagine the Palace of Versailles was to anyone who wandered its gilded halls just prior to the French revolution. To be clear, this isn't any sort of slight on the devs who'll no doubt have worked hard to bring this system and others in GTA 6 to life, a number of whom have a recoginition vote on their unionisation efforts coming up next month.

From a player perspective, one can only hope that by the time GTA 6 hits PC, the RAM crisis has led hardware makers to invest heavily in smellivision tech, so that players around the world can drink in the guffs causing their butt naked on-screen analogue's eyes to water or revel in the stink caused by hitting someone with a bag of dog shit. Forget AI bollocks, this is the future, I scream as I retch into a toilet bowl while some funky tunes from Justice play in the background.

#4205. Father Arrested For Leaving 6-Year-Old Daughter Sleeping In Line For Pokémon Cards

A 35-year-old South Carolina man has been arrested and accused of leaving his 6-year-old daughter asleep while waiting in line for Pokémon cards.

As reported by The Washington Post (thanks, IGN), John-Michael Dooley was waiting outside a Target store with his daughter in Charleston's West Ashley district, where a crowd had gathered hoping to purchase the newly-released Pokémon set. Officers arrived at the store at 2:30am local time after receiving reports of an unattended child.

Witnesses reported that Dooley gave his daughter a pillow and a blanket sometime after 1:00am before leaving her asleep in the line. After he failed to return within an hour, the concerned witnesses contacted the police.

When the man eventually returned to the store, he was arrested. He later admitted to leaving his daughter unattended so that he could keep his place in line while he had gone home. He was subsequently charged with unlawful conduct toward a child, while his daughter was placed in emergency protective custody. Thankfully, she was unharmed.

Many of us here at NL are parents, and so it enrages us to no end that someone would even consider doing this. We're at least relieved that no harm came to the 6-year-old girl, but it could have been much worse.

In the words of Reggie Fils-Aimé... "What's wrong with you?"

#4204. Forza Horizon 6's New City Life Update Includes Multiple Halo & Xbox Freebies

Unlock Master Chief, liveries and the Xbox IKEA Prop Pack!

Yesterday marked the long-awaited arrival of Forza Horizon 6's City Life update, which adds two new permanent race routes in Tokyo City amongst other things, and there are even some Xbox and Halo-related freebies tucked in!

In terms of Halo, it's said that everyone will soon be getting a free 2025 GR GT Prototype livery via the Message Centre celebrating the franchise along with Xbox's 25th anniversary. We haven't come across this yet, although we did get a separate Master Chief livery for the Urus Lamborghini as well.

Meanwhile, Master Chief himself will become available as a character model in the Week 2 Photo Challenge.

"Additionally, join us in celebrating 25 Years of XBOX and Halo with a special livery on the 2025 GR GT Prototype (to be sent to all players via Message Center) and The Master Chief Outfit unlockable in the Week 2 Photo Challenge of the Festival Playlist."

Beyond this, they've also added an IKEA Prop Pack containing items from the recent real-life collaboration with Xbox that you can use to decorate your custom garages, so that's a neat little addition.

As for the more meaty stuff, you'll find 3 new-to-Horizon cars in the Festival Playlist, while the two new race routes arrive in the form of the Edo Circuit Road Race and Shuto Charge Street Race.

Most of this is available to check out in Forza Horizon 6 right now, although as mentioned, the Halo livery for the GR GT Prototype and Master Chief character skin haven't arrived just yet. Plenty to be getting on with in the meantime!

#4203. Call of Duty: Modern Warfare 4 intro cinematic is "not intended to reference or trivialise" real-world South Korean crowd crush, Activision say amid reported backlash

Update: Activision reportedly confirm footage will be removed in November Modern Warfare 4 update

Update: The BBC report that Activision have issued a statement apologising to the victims of the Itaewon crowd crush and confirmed that the news footage from the disaster in Modern Warfare 4's intro cinematic will be removed. An update coming to the shooter on November 12th will do the deed.

The 10.29 Itaewon Disaster Bereaved Families Association have welcomed Activision's decision to pull the footage, according to the BBC, but also said they hadn't received a direct apology from the Call of Duty publishers.

The intro cinematic of Call of Duty: Modern Warfare 4, this year's Activision mil-shooter, has reportedly caused controversy in South Korea due to the use of some real world news footage from a 2022 crowd crush in Seoul's Itaewon district which killed around 150 people. Activision have now issued a response to the situation, in which they state the intro is "not intended to reference or trivialise the Itaewon disaster or any other real-world tragedy".

Korean site SBS News have reported on the backlash Modern Warfare 4's opening cinematic has caused in the country. Their story - which it's worth noting has been translated into English by AI, and thus is acknowledged as potentially containing errors - claimed that the shooter's intro features three seconds of real-world broadcast footage showing a emergency workers performing CPR on a collapsed person during the Itaewon crowd crush's aftermath.

The crush saw a crowd of people become trapped in a narrow alleyway during Halloween weekend celebrations in the South Korean capital, with between 150 and 160 people dying as a result of becoming so tightly packed together that some couldn't breathe. According to the report, groups and bodies in Korea including an association representing families who suffered bereavements in the crush have called for Activision to remove the footage from Modern Warfare 4's intro.

Approached for comment by RPS, Activision issued the following statement on the situation:

Modern Warfare 4's campaign is built around a North Korean invasion of South Korea.

#4202. Stalker 2’s first expansion officially revealed, and it's taking us to the power plant where it all began

Stalker 2’s first add-on isn’t far off, and it may just be the thing to bring you back to post-apocalyptic Chornobyl in 2026.

One of the biggest reveals out of today’s Xbox Partner Preview showcase has been the new Stalker 2 expansion. The developer did tease some sort of announcement ahead of the event, but I don’t think an expansion was on many of our bingo cards.

Cost of Hope is the big news; a new add-on that the developer has wisely decided to reveal fairly close to release. Or, at least, the planned release target.

First off, Cost of Hope is set for release this summer. It’ll arrive on all current platforms simultaneously, meaning PC, Xbox, and PlayStation. The expansion is described as “non-linear”, and it takes place in the heartlands, deeper into the Zone.

The story revolves around a conflict between Duty, and Freedom, two factions whose idea of the what the Zone is and their understanding of its possibilities differ widely. You’ll be playing as protagonist Skif once again, and the expansion’s events will run parallel to the main game.

GSC Game World says Cost of Hope will introduce two new regions, offering dozens of hours of gameplay. We’ll get to actually explore the Chornobyl Nuclear Power Plant as part of the expansion, alongside the Iron Forest.

Each of the two new regions will have its own hub area, NPCs, quests, activities and stories. Of course, it wouldn’t be a Stalker expansion without some new weapons, and Cost of Hope promises a few - some can even be seen in the trailer.

The developer also confirmed that there’s one other story DLC in the works. Together with Heart of Chornobyl, and Cost of Hope all three will form a trilogy of interconnected stories. More details on Cost of Hope - including a release date - will be revealed sometime in the summer.
